News.title: Body of woman in her 70s found in park as cops fear victim could have been dead for weeks before tragic discovery
News.content:
MURDER PROBE Body of woman in her 70s found in park as cops fear victim could have been dead for weeks before tragic discovery

A WOMAN’S body has been found in a park and is feared to have been there “a number of weeks” as cops launch a murder investigation.

The victim, in her 70s, was found in Stanley Park, Liverpool, yesterday at around 5:25pm.

She has been described as white with strawberry blonde hair, but is yet to be identified.

Police believe the deceased woman may have been there for a number of weeks.





A post-mortem has taken place today, but results are being withheld for investigative reasons.

A murder probe has now been launched and police are urging anyone with information to get in touch.

Enquiries remain ongoing to identify her and inform her next of kin.

Detective Superintendent Rachel Wilson said: “We understand that this will be distressing and worrying for people to hear and I want the local community to be reassured that we are doing everything in our powers to find the person or persons responsible and bring them to justice.



“We have carried out a number of lines of enquiry, including examining any missing people reports in the Merseyside and wider area, but at this stage we have not been able to identify the woman and would ask for the public’s help by coming forward with any information.

“We know she is a white woman, aged in her 70s, approximately 5ft 2in tall, of small build with strawberry blonde hair.

“When she was found she was wearing a distinctive cerise pink Nike T-shirt.”

The force has asked for any walkers or dog walkers who have been nearby in recent weeks to get in touch.

News.title: How Scotland’s gang war is sparking ‘unfair punishment’ among cons in notorious Scots jail
News.content:
PRISONERS in a notorious jail with feared mobsters have moaned that it is unfair how they all get punished over gang bust-ups — even those not involved.

They claimed authorities at HMP Low Moss come down too hard when blood is spilled behind bars, including ordering them all to eat alone in their cells for up to a week.



The string of gripes emerged following violence as the underworld was gripped by a turf war linked to caged cocaine kingpin Mark Richardson, 39 — an inmate at the overcrowded nick in Bishopbriggs, near Glasgow.

One disgruntled inmate told of being “unfairly” disciplined over clashes between rivals.

He told inspectors: “If there is a fight in the section, anyone involved gets put on a rule which is fair.



“But then the other 30-odd prisoners have to deal with ‘rec or snack’ and dine-ins for seven days even though they played no part. Unfairly punishing people makes no sense.”

Another fed-up lag echoed his moans about being forced to take meals in cells. He said it was unfair that “people that are not involved in the fight get punished for it”.

Others were more complimentary about conditions with one saying: “The majority of staff members here are respectful, helpful and caring.”



But another frustrated con whinged: “Everyone gets punished for two other people fighting.”

The concerns emerged in a report by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Prisons in Scotland. It uncovered worries about the large number of cons with ties to organised crime crews.

The document also pinpointed unease about how rival thugs were being held in the same prison — where “enemies and mixed regimes” could be found.

Inspectors visited in August last year — five months after the gang war kicked off when firebomber Logan Carlin, 26, torched a beauty salon in Edinburgh’s Leith linked to Richardson.

It was the first in a wave of attacks by Tamo Junto maniacs allegedly ordered by ex-Union Bears ultra Ross ‘Miami’ McGill, 32.



He blamed Richardson’s lackeys for ripping him off with fake cash in a £500,000 cocaine deal.

The mayhem spread to Glasgow as the notorious Daniel crime clan were targeted by hoods with ties to their enemies in the Lyons mob.

Cops went on to nail a wave of thugs through their Operation Portaledge probe into the mayhem.

Last August, six of Richardson’s crew were locked up for a total of 101 years.

They included Michael Heeps, 35, whose reign of terror included murder bids and torching the cars of prison guards.



We told in November how Richardson was placed in solitary confinement at Low Moss amid fears for his safety.

But the Inspectorate report has given the jail a “satisfactory” rating for how it tackled trouble through “violence reduction measures”.

And it said attacks were being “consistently monitored and reviewed” along with concerns about drug smuggling and staff shortages.

Inspectors concluded: “A range of challenges included high prisoner numbers, cell sharing, the number of organised crime group nominals, together with enemies and mixed regimes, the introduction of illicit substances, and staff shortages.

“To combat the levels of violence, the establishment had implemented further measures.



“Powers to confine prisoners to their cell, to segregate them, or limit their opportunities to associate with others are exercised appropriately and in accordance with the law.

“The focus was on reintegration.”

Police Scotland Chief Constable Jo Farrell has since claimed in her annual performance report that the gang feud has now ended after rivals groups had reached a “resolution of differences”.

But Graeme Pearson, former head of the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency, warned the violence would continue to spill over in jail halls.

The ex-cop said: “We have a lot of competitors in prison — and there is no doubt there will be frictions arising as a result of that.”

News.title: Man, 49, seriously injured after ‘emergency’ on 147ft rollercoaster in Madrid as thrillseeker airlifted to hospital
News.content:
RIDE DANGER Man, 49, seriously injured after ‘emergency’ on 147ft rollercoaster in Madrid as thrillseeker airlifted to hospital

A MAN was rushed to hospital with horrific leg injuries after a shock incident on a Batman rollercoaster at a Spanish theme park.

The victim, 49, was caught up in the terrifying incident at Warner Bros. Park in San Martín de la Vega, Madrid, on Saturday.



Emergency crews raced to the scene before airlifting the stricken man to Madrid’s 12 de Octubre Hospital with a “potentially serious” prognosis.

The shocking accident happened on Batman Gotham City Escape, a monster 45-metre-high ride which opened in 2023.



The man suffered an open fracture to his left leg and a closed fracture to his right, leaving him with a “potentially serious” prognosis.

The thrill ride plunges passengers down a brutal 98-degree drop, fires them through multiple launches and sends them hurtling at more than 100km/h.



The rollercoaster was immediately stopped and emergency procedures were activated, according to Warner Bros. Park.

The injured man was treated at the scene by emergency teams before being evacuated by helicopter.

The attraction has since been shut to the public while the incident is investigated alongside the authorities.

Witnesses described the aftermath as chaotic, with screams alerting people waiting near the ride.



Noelia Hans, 21, said the scene left visitors “completely shocked” and that they left the park “deeply shaken”.

Laura Muñoz claimed visitors did not see “any safety or evacuation protocols” as dozens remained in the waiting area in darkness and amid shouts.

She said she and six colleagues, all military personnel, searched for an emergency exit before helping other visitors, particularly children, escape.



Muñoz also claimed there were “very distressed people who didn’t receive adequate attention”.

She said a manager offered no explanation and “simply offered them a fast-track pass to return another day.”

Despite the frightening incident, the rest of the park continued operating almost normally, with other rides still running around two hours later.

Batman Gotham City Escape remained firmly closed as Civil Guard and Local Police vehicles were deployed at the entrance.

By shortly before 6pm, dozens of onlookers had gathered outside the ride, with some apparently unaware of the earlier horror and left wondering why it was shut.



The park’s app still listed the attraction as open, although it showed no waiting time.

Behind the barriers, the thunder of the coaster could still be heard as cars raced along the track.

Empty seats periodically emerged in what appeared to be operational tests, despite the ride remaining closed to visitors.

The park, around 25km from Madrid, has suffered another deadly ride tragedy in the past.

In 2005, a 22-year-old man died after an accident on the Haunted Hotel attraction.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The park said at the time that he had stood up after suffering a panic attack and struck his head, while his family claimed the safety bar had malfunctioned and could be lifted without difficulty.

The latest incident has now left Batman Gotham City Escape under investigation.

News.title: Why Britain must stop focusing on the cost of living and start rewarding work again
News.content:
Sir Keir Starmer's former Cost of Living Tsar issues a blunt message for the new PM in a bombshell intervention ahead of the Budget

RICHARD WALKER Why Britain must stop focusing on the cost of living and start rewarding work again

It’s time for British politics to stop focusing on the cost of living and start focusing on the cost of getting Britain back to work.

That’s my view as a businessman and the former Government’s Cost of Living Champion, where I argued strongly for more targeted help for families who simply could not absorb soaring household bills.

That was the right thing to do, but now we need to face our uncomfortable truth head on.



We cannot fix the cost of living as Bailout Britain – in which every problem is answered with another subsidy, benefit or demand on businesses to pick up the bill.



Because ultimately there is only one sustainable answer to the cost-of-living crisis: a country that grows, creates good jobs and allows people to keep more of what they earn.

That is why I welcome Andy Burnham saying he wants to be a pro-business Prime Minister.

He is right to talk about investment and wealth creation. Britain badly needs both.

But warm words towards business won’t be enough.

The Prime Minister and his new Chancellor, John Healey, now need to be brave enough to change the direction of the economy.

And their first priority should be simple: make it cheaper to employ people, invest and grow.



Businesses do not create jobs in a vacuum.

Every rise in employers’ National Insurance, every punishing business rates bill, and every other additional cost imposed by Whitehall changes the calculation about whether to create another job.

Those decisions multiplied across every business in the country determine whether Britain grows or stagnates.

So the October Budget should begin shifting the tax burden away from jobs and productive investment.



Cut the cost of employing people and go further on business rates.

Give companies the confidence that if they invest in Britain today, government will not simply come back and tax that investment tomorrow.

The fact is that successful businesses do more to remove poverty than any support programme can.

It’s time to make the brave decisions on welfare and use that money to boost business confidence and, ultimately, generate the taxes that pay for our schools, hospitals and public services.

I learnt that lesson early in my career, establishing a business in Poland – a country that has since spent decades investing, building infrastructure, developing skills, attracting businesses and integrating itself into global supply chains.



This month, S&P Dow Jones Indices announced that Poland would be upgraded to developed-market status.

Britain needs some of that hunger again and nowhere is that more urgent than with our young people.

The latest figures show 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 are not in employment, education or training.



Yes, that number has finally fallen below a million. But it is still 30,000 higher than a year ago.

As a father, that horrifies me.

Behind that statistic are hundreds of thousands of young lives at risk of starting adulthood without the routine, confidence, skills, friendships and sense of purpose that work can provide.

I believe work is a moral mission. Good work gives people independence and dignity and long periods without it are associated with poverty and poorer mental and physical health.

Of course there will always be people who are ill, disabled or facing circumstances in which the state must support them. A decent society protects them.



But compassion also means recognising that the welfare state should be a safety net and a springboard, not a system that leaves people who can work parked on benefits and written off.

We need dramatically better routes from school into work: proper apprenticeships, vocational training and work experience developing skills that employers actually need.

I therefore welcome the Prime Minister’s focus this week on creating more work placements.

But businesses will create far more opportunities if government removes the barriers stopping them from hiring in the first place.

Lower the cost of creating jobs, help businesses invest in skills, and make sure work always pays.



We must always give young people a real route into those jobs and stop entry jobs being replaced by AI.

Do that and Britain gets a triple dividend.

People move from welfare into wages. the benefits bill falls and tax revenues rise.

Businesses gain the people and skills they need to grow and, most importantly, a generation currently being offered too little hope gets a stake in the country’s future.

I know how painful the cost-of-living crisis has been.



But the biggest mistake we could make now would be to confuse helping people through a crisis with accepting the conditions that created it.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Britain cannot redistribute its way to prosperity; we have to build our way there.

Andy Burnham says he wants to get Britain’s economy moving again. Now he and the Chancellor must prove they are prepared to make the difficult choices required to do it.

News.title: Andy Burnham must cut taxes on business to get Brits to work and boost growth, former Cost of Living Czar warns
News.content:
Labour peer Richard Walker - who runs Iceland supermarket - has become the latest business figure to warn the PM he must cut taxes on business to turn the UK's sluggish economy around

BUDGET WARNING Andy Burnham must cut taxes on business to get Brits to work and boost growth, former Cost of Living Czar warns

THE GOVERNMENT’S former Cost of Living Czar today tells Andy Burnham to cut business taxes in the Budget to create jobs and growth.

In an explosive intervention, Richard Walker said No10 should “stop focusing on the cost of living and start focusing on the cost of getting Britain back to work”.

Lord Walker is a Labour peer who served as Sir Keir Starmer’s Cost of Living adviser and is chairman of the Iceland supermarket.



But in a bombshell article, he says the time for bailouts is over and the government must cut the costs on businesses to turn the economy around.



This will cut the benefits bill, tackle the youth unemployment crisis and make struggling Brits better off, he said.

Lord Walker warned “warm words towards business won’t be enough” and the PM and Chancellor John Healey must cut business taxes in the Budget in October.

Writing in today’s Sun on Sunday, he said: “Their first priority should be simple: make it cheaper to employ people, invest and grow.



“Every rise in employers’ National Insurance, every punishing business rates bill, and every other additional cost imposed by Whitehall changes the calculation about whether to create another job.

“The October Budget should begin shifting the tax burden away from jobs and productive investment.

“Cut the cost of employing people and go further on business rates.

“Give companies the confidence that if they invest in Britain today, the government will not simply come back and tax investment tomorrow.”



The Labour peer and supermarket boss spent six months advising Sir Keir on how to help Brits clobbered by crippling price rises.

He said he knows “how painful the cost of living crisis has been”, but added: “We need to face our uncomfortable truth head on.

“We cannot fix the cost of living as bailout Britain – in which every problem is answered with another subsidy, benefit or demand on business to pick up the bill.”



Lord Walker also called for “brave decisions on welfare” to get Brits back into work and ease the bloated benefits bill.

Lord Walker was made a Labour member of the House of Lords by Sir Keir.

He quit his role the day before Mr Burnham became PM, having given his report and recommendations to Sir Keir.

Mr Burnham is preparing to unveil his first Budget as PM on October 28, and is expected to raise taxes.

But a growing number of business chiefs and economists have warned that hiking levies further will backfire and harm UK plc.



This includes Jim O’Neill, a former banker and Burnham ally who has warned it would be “stupid ” to raise wealth taxes in the Budget.

Britain’s tax burden is already at its highest level since the Second World War, and the employer NICs hike has been blamed for job losses and poor growth.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mr Burnham has vowed to be a “pro business PM” and said he wants to ease the burden of doing business in the UK.

His looming economic blueprint is being seen as a key test of that promise.

News.title: Shameless Putin says he is killer whale ‘tearing polar bear to pieces’ as he desperately tries to justify Ukraine war
News.content:
A DERANGED Vladimir Putin has bizarrely compared himself to a killer whale tearing a polar bear “to pieces” to try and justify his invasion of Ukraine.

The Russian tyrant launched into the crazed tirade while speaking to trainee educators on their first day of school.



He asked one student, who said they had visited the North Pole, if he had seen any polar bears – to which the they replied: “Yes, of course.”

Putin replied: “Can you imagine, and right there, nearby, there are killer whales? They eat these bears like small fry.



“Yeah… they just pounce in a pack and boom, they tear them to pieces.”

The unhinged rant at the Moscow State Pedagogical University then swerved into a dubious biology lesson.



Continuing with his sickening comments, he said: “It’s all very interesting. Yes, yes, yes. That’s the food chain.

“Children need to be told about this too, so they understand the world we live in and why we’re conducting a Special Military Operation.”

The “Special Military Operation” is Putin’s unique way of describing his bloodthirsty war on Ukraine which has so far claimed 1.5million lives.

Human rights activist Olga Romanovam said it was “one of Putin’s craziest monologues — killer whales attack bears, so we conduct a special military operation.”



Ukraine Fights Telegram channel said: “Putin no longer even tries to hide how distorted his perception of the world is. He’s simply an animal.”

The ruthless war chief appears to have been hoodwinked by fake AI videos showing orcas ripping into the multi-hundred-kilo beasts.

Putin’s polar bear orca attacks have been debunked in the BBC‘s Discover Wildlife magazine which wrote: “There are no confirmed records of orcas hunting polar bears (although plenty of fake AI videos trying to spread this false news).”



The tyrant also praised the brutal practice of some northern peoples of abandoning their eldery to be eaten by wolves.

He shamelessly told teachers: “Yes, it all looks harsh, but that’s how their life is.”

It comes as Russia ramps up its attacks on Ukraine – and executes brutal double-tap strickes on busy shopping malls and residential streets.

Today the tyrant’s forces bombed a Ukrainian ammo dump – and triggered a deadly fireball which killed 37.

The blitz on Mila on the outskirts of Kyiv was the deadliest strike on Ukraine so far this year.



A further 42 people have been confirmed as injured in the horror blast.

Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko called it an “irreparable loss”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “Unfortunately, there are fatalities as a result of the enemy attack.

“I express my sincere condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed.”

News.title: Norway mourns King Harald V as thousands gather at royal palace to bid farewell to monarch after his death at 89
News.content:
THOUSANDS of grieving Norwegians have flooded Oslo to bid a heartbreaking farewell to King Harald V after the beloved monarch died aged 89.

Mourners have packed the streets outside the Royal Palace, where Harald’s coffin now lies in state, clutching flowers, cards, drawings and Norwegian flags.



Europe’s oldest reigning monarch died peacefully on Friday after a final battle with haemolytic anaemia, bringing his 35-year reign to a sombre end.

His death has plunged the Scandinavian nation into mourning, with flags dramatically lowered to half-mast and huge portraits of the late king appearing across the country.



On Friday night, huge crowds braved pouring rain to watch Harald’s funeral cortege make its solemn journey from Oslo University Hospital to the palace.

More than 20,000 people had already paid their respects by Saturday after floral tributes began piling up outside the royal residence.

Harald was widely admired for his warmth, humility and fiercely inclusive approach to modern Norway.

One mourner, Bulgarian-born teacher Veselina Vitanova, 43, said: “He meant a lot to us immigrants … We felt really very included. So, thanks to him, I feel so Norwegian.”

Another remembered Harald’s powerful 2016 speech, which went viral around the world.

The late king famously said: “Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys and girls and boys who love each other”.



Mari Eidsvaag, 32, wore a T-shirt emblazoned with the words, a rainbow and a drawing of Harald.

“It embodies the way he felt about people and the way he wanted us Norwegians to feel about each other,” she said.

“I think it’s a very important statement, especially these days.”



Harald was also praised for helping unite the country after the devastating 2011 massacre carried out by neo-Nazi Anders Behring Breivik, which killed 77 people.

Caroline Vagle, a reporter for Se og Hor, said Harald “was someone who always seemed to find the words that brought us together and gave us a sense of security”.

The death of Harald has triggered an immediate royal succession, with his 53-year-old son automatically becoming king.

He will reign as King Haakon VIII, taking over a monarchy celebrated for its modernity and modesty but rocked by a string of recent scandals.

“The king is dead. Long live the king,” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said after meeting the new monarch.



Haakon addressed the nation in a televised speech at 7pm local time on Saturday.

The King said: “Dear father, thank you for being a good father to Martha and me.

“You were the head of the family.”

He swore an oath before parliament on Tuesday, pledging to defend Norway’s constitution and laws.

There will be no coronation, with the centuries-old practice abolished by parliament in 1908.



Instead, Haakon could choose to have his reign blessed in a ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral.

King Charles has paid an emotional tribute to his “dear cousin” following Harald’s death.

In a statement released by Buckingham Palace, he said: “It is with the most profound sadness that my wife and I have learned of the death of my dear cousin, King Harald V of Norway.”



He added: “For 35 years, King Harald served his people with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility.”

Charles said Harald was a “much-loved kinsman and friend” whose “kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty” stretched “across the sea and across the decades”.

He also highlighted the “particularly close historical and family ties” between Britain and Norway.

“The Queen and I extend our deepest and most heartfelt condolences to Queen Sonja and all her family, as Britain shares in Norway’s grief at this time of such heartbreaking loss.”

He signed the message: “Charles R.”



Harald had suffered mounting health problems in recent years and had been in hospital in Oslo since August 17.

He had been treated with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a rare condition in which red blood cells are destroyed unusually quickly, causing fatigue and shortness of breath.

His final years were dogged by repeated hospital stays.

Earlier this year he was rushed for medical treatment in Tenerife after falling ill while on holiday, while in 2024 he was hospitalised in Malaysia with an infection and fitted with a temporary pacemaker.

A permanent pacemaker was later implanted in Norway.



The royal household subsequently announced a “permanent reduction” in Harald’s public engagements “out of consideration for his age”.

But the monarch always ruled out abdicating, insisting he had made a lifelong oath before parliament.

His death comes as the wider royal family faces fresh turmoil.



Queen Sonja, also 89, was briefly hospitalised in May with heart problems.

Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, has faced scrutiny over her ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Her son Marius Borg Hoiby was sentenced in June to four years in prison for two rapes.

Mette-Marit, 53, has also battled serious pulmonary fibrosis and underwent a lung transplant in July.

Harald was just three when Nazi Germany invaded Norway during the Second World War.



He and his sisters, Princesses Ragnhild and Astrid, were forced to flee, eventually spending five years in the United States after being granted political asylum.

Before taking the throne, Harald was a passionate athlete and Olympic sailor who competed at multiple Games.

He later won numerous international regattas, including the World Championships in sailing in 1987.

He became king in 1991 following the death of his father, Olav V, and spent more than three decades steering Norway through enormous social change.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Store described him as “a king of his time and for his time”.



He said Harald had accompanied Norway as the country “grew richer, we became more numerous, and we became more diverse”.

News.title: Man in his 30s left fighting for his life in hospital after serious street assault in London as cops issue urgent appeal
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

ASSAULT HORROR Man in his 30s left fighting for his life in hospital after serious street assault in London as cops issue urgent appeal

A MAN has been left fighting for his life after a “serious” assault in north London as police issue an urgent appeal.

Cops were called to a street in Stratford following reports of an attack at around 9pm.

An emergency response team showed up at Penny Brookes Street where they found the man, in his 30s, in critical condition.

The individual was taken to hospital where he remains in life-threatening condition.





It is believed the suspects fled the scene prior to cops arriving.

No arrests have been made at this point, and police enquiries are ongoing.

Detective Sergeant Justina Rackauskaite said: “A man remains in hospital with life-threatening injuries following this assault, and our investigation is progressing at pace to establish the circumstances leading up to this incident.

“We have conducted a range of enquiries and are now appealing for the public’s help.

“We are particularly keen to hear from anyone who was in the Penny Brookes Street area that evening and may have seen something.

“I would also urge anyone with CCTV, doorbell camera or dashcam footage that could assist our enquiries, to contact us.”

Anyone with information should call police on 101 quoting CAD 3842/28AUG or call Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Burscough train crash - updates: One dead after train hits van near Liverpool
News.content:
Paramedics and fire crews surrounded a Northern train in West Lancashire after it collided with a van at a level crossing, leaving one dead and two injured

A man has died and two others have been injured after a train struck a van at a railway crossing in West Lancashire.

The Northern train had come to halt next to green fields in the Burscough area, with multiple ambulances and a fire engine dispatched to the scene.

One passenger posted an image of a damaged carriage with debris strewn across the floor. The passenger said they were still on the train with their children, adding "we are all shook".

The incident appears to have unfolded near Martin Lane in Burscough, near its junction with Whitehouse Lane, reports the Liverpool Echo.

Northern has blocked all lines between Wigan Wallgate and Southport "due to emergency services dealing with an incident," with disruption expected for the rest of the day.

The company said: "Northern train ticket restrictions have been lifted in the affected areas, including Advance and Peak restrictions, during this disruption. Restrictions will be reinstated once the disruption ends."

News.title: Scandal-hit baby death hospital trust ex-chief's firm raked in THOUSANDS providing NHS maternity training
News.content:
The ex-boss of a scandal-hit health trust exposed over baby deaths co-owns a firm which raked in cash giving maternity training to the NHS.

A senior midwife’s inquiry into Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust found 520 mothers and babies suffered potentially avoidable harm or death due to poor care. Now it can be revealed former long-serving CEO Peter Homa is director of a company paid nearly £100,000 for maternity training provided to another Trust.

And we can disclose Dr Homa, who joined the NHS in 1979, racked up a pension pot worth more than £2million before retiring in 2017. Unveiling her landmark review, which covered the experiences of families mostly from 2012 to 2025, Donna Ockenden said in June: “This report is about what happens when leadership fails.”

View 6 Images Sarah and Jack Hawkins, whose daughter Harriet died in the womb in 2016 following maternity staff mistakes, said: 'Peter Homa was CEO when so much death and harm occurred at NUH...' (Image: Jacob King/PA Wire)

‌



The Lib Dems’ Health and Social Care Spokesperson Helen Morgan MP said: “It is frankly shocking that a firm now co-owned by someone who presided over such catastrophic failures in maternity care has been handed cash to deliver maternity governance training to the NHS.

“The Ockenden review laid bare the horrific trauma suffered by mothers and babies at Nottingham University Hospitals, alongside a culture where staff concerns were ignored and systemic failures were hidden. The public will rightly question how NHS trusts can justify using public funds in this manner.”

Sarah and Jack Hawkins, awarded a £2.8m settlement after their daughter Harriet died in the womb following maternity staff mistakes at Nottingham City Hospital in 2016, said: “Peter Homa was CEO when so much death and harm occurred at NUH as shown by the Ockenden review and by so many brave families who have told what happened to them…

“We are very confused to hear he is selling leadership development. To us, it doesn’t seem right that someone with his track record should be running a company paid large sums of money to offer leadership training to the NHS or anybody, frankly.”

‌



View 6 Images Gary and Sarah Andrews, whose daughter Wynter died 23 minutes after being born in 2019 following care failings, said: 'We know the consequences when leadership and culture fail.' (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

And Sarah and Gary Andrews, whose daughter Wynter died 23 minutes after being born in 2019 at the Trust’s Queen’s Medical Centre following care failings, said: “It is… difficult for us to understand how his private firm can now provide leadership training to the NHS. We know from the Ockenden Review that there were serious concerns about leadership, culture and the failure to keep women and babies safe during his tenure.

“We are not saying that one individual was responsible for every failure identified by Ockenden, but we believe it is entirely legitimate for families to question whether someone who led the organisation during such a troubled period is well placed to provide leadership training to future NHS leaders.

“For us, leadership is not simply about management theory or training courses. We know the consequences when leadership and culture fail. We are living those consequences. We have lost babies, our children have been harmed and our lives have been permanently changed. It therefore does not sit comfortably with us that someone who was at the helm during a period in which such serious failures occurred can now be paid substantial sums from public money to help shape the leadership of the NHS.”

‌



View 6 Images Dr Peter Homa joined the NHS in 1979

Dr Homa has been director and co-owner of Acorn Leadership Development since 2024. The firm’s website, which carries his picture, boasts its “focus is on helping you develop and nurture the leaders you need to navigate the challenges you face”. University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire Trust paid the firm £45,372 in September last year for nursing training, transparency data showed.

In March last year, Acorn was also paid £98,250 for “training course fees/exps” relating to “maternity governance”, according to Northampton General Hospital spending data. And, the same month, the spending data shows it was handed £28,600 for “training course fees/exps” relating to “clinical placement”.

In a case study section of Acorn’s website, the firm details its work for an NHS Hospital leadership team. It says: “Our client was experiencing ongoing challenges with ED [emergency department] access and waiting times, as well as patient experience and quality of care… We were asked to deliver a leadership development programme to help these newly established teams build trusted relationships and a shared leadership purpose."

‌



View 6 Images Unveiling her landmark review, Donna Ockenden said in June: 'This report is about what happens when leadership fails.' (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

By April 2016, the cash equivalent of Dr Homa’s pension was £2,066,000, NUH accounts showed. The one-time hospital porter spent the majority of his career working in the NHS.

Dr Homa’s Facebook profile showed he has a taste for adventure, with a photo of him thrusting his fist in the air on a bridge climb in Sydney, Australia. In another snap, the 69-year-old, who lives in Leicestershire, posed in an apron in the kitchen. “I'm the cook at home and find it therapeutic,” he wrote in a comment in 2014.

After leaving Nottingham, he had a stint as chair of NHS Leadership Academy. Dr Homa, who says he wanted to be a pilot but could not because of sight loss in one eye, once wrote a letter to his younger self. “You will face many leadership challenges and how you respond creates your personal brand and legacy,” he said.

‌



And he said: “You will get things wrong and fail. Failure is another way to learn…Be a leader in openness. Acknowledge failure, when it occurs, and do what needs to be done to prevent repetition… In the words of philosophers, Friedrich Nietzsche and Kelly Clarkson, 'What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger…'”

View 6 Images Dr Homa has told of his 'profound sadness on reading the findings of the review' (Image: FACEBOOK)

Dr Homa was also director general of the Defence Medical Services, which cares for armed forces personnel, from 2019 to 2023. Ms Ockenden’s review, the largest maternity inquiry in NHS history, published devastating findings.

The inquiry found leaders at the Trust knew there were serious issues in the maternity department going back years – yet failed to take action to stop more deaths. Over 2,000 families and more than 800 members of staff past and present contributed to the inquiry, with the Trust already paying out millions in compensation and fines after being prosecuted for poor care.

‌



The University Hospitals of Northamptonshire (UHN) Group Managing Director and Chief Nurse Julie Hogg said: “We can confirm that multi-professional members of our team have undertaken leadership development training delivered by Acorn. We are satisfied that the programme was delivered to the required standards and has supported the ongoing professional development of our staff.” Dr Homa “delivered a virtual leadership talk of around one hour”, with different sessions “facilitated by others”, a spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust said: “Experienced trainers from Acorn Leadership Development were used to train our senior perinatal team. Independent evaluation of the programme has been positive, and this investment forms part of our wider focus on maintaining safe, high-quality services.” Dr Homa did not personally deliver leadership training at the Trust, a spokesperson said. However, they added that he attended “one session focused on the importance of speaking up and escalating concerns but was not paid for this”.

NUH’s chief nurse Tracy Pilcher said: "We recognise the importance of the Independent Maternity Review and fully accept the failings outlined by Donna Ockenden, for which we are truly sorry. We remain committed to implementing all immediate and essential actions to support the improvement of our services. We continue to work closing [sic] with the harmed and bereaved families and Donna Ockenden to ensure we have learned all lessons from the review.”

Dr Homa is understood to have limited day-to-day involvement with Acorn, from which has received £2,000 in dividends. The ex-CEO, who has faced a call to be stripped of his CBE, has admitted families were let down but said he did not recognise some of the Ockenden report findings on an executive level culture of fear.

‌



Last month, he told the Sunday Times of his "profound sadness on reading the findings of the review", adding: "The families directly and indirectly affected by the service failings at NUH have my deepest, most sincere apologies." Dr Homa and Acorn were contacted for comment.

News.title: Middlesbrough - live: Football fans honour cops killed in wrong-way A66 crash at home game
News.content:
Middlesbrough FC supporters have paid tribute to two police officers killed in the A66 crash as Cleveland Police continues an operation against organised crime.

Debris left following memorial for man who died in A66 crash

Middlesbrough FC supporters have paid tribute to PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, who were killed in last weekend’s wrong-way A66 crash.

Pictures of the two officers were displayed on screens at the Riverside Stadium before Saturday’s home game against West Bromwich Albion, with players and supporters joining in a round of applause.

Police said on Friday that seven more men had been arrested as part of an operation against organised crime following the A66 crash, which led to the deaths of two police officers and five young males.

It means Cleveland Police has now arrested 24 people since the collision between a marked police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat near Middlesbrough last Saturday.

However, the force also confirmed detectives are not linking a fatal house fire which killed a seven-year-old girl and her aunt to last weekend’s deadly A66 crash.

On Wednesday, Valentina Foster, seven, and her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, were tragically killed in a house fire in Grangetown on Teesside. Two men have since been arrested on suspicion of murder.

Following that, on Thursday morning a wall at a house in South Bank was allegedly rammed by a car. Some of the latest arrests relate to this incident.

Separately, footage shared online showed a number of cars on fire in a field in Haswell, County Durham, as balloons were released at a memorial event for Michael Robert Cahill, 23, one of the five men in the Passat. It appeared the cars - including an £80K Porsche - were set ablaze as part of the event.

News.title: Reform council blasted over desperate £150,000 stunt for 'operatives' to monitor migrants
News.content:
Reform council blasted over desperate £150,000 stunt for 'operatives' to monitor migrants

Essex County Council said the 'operatives' would be sent to town and city centres in Braintree, Colchester and Chelmsford where migrants can visit from a nearby accommodation centre

View 2 Images Wethersfield, a former airbase in Essex, has been used to house asylum seekers since 2023 (Image: PA)

A Reform-led council has been accused of a desperate stunt over plans to spend £150,000 to deploy security guards to monitor asylum seekers.

‌



Essex County Council said the “operatives” would be sent to town and city centres in Braintree, Colchester and Chelmsford where migrants can visit from a nearby accommodation centre.

‌



MDP Wethersfield, a former airbase near Halstead in north Essex, has been used to house single male migrants since 2023. Numbers of people at the site are expected to grow from 800 to 1,220 as the Government pushes to end the costly use of asylum hotels to house migrants.

‌



But the move was quickly exposed as hollow as private security guards will have no more power than ordinary members of the public, and law enforcement will still need to be led by police.

View 2 Images Liberal Democrat MP for Chelmsford Marie Goldman accused the council of stoking division (Image: PA)

Essex council claimed there was “anecdotal evidence” that “the presence of this community of asylum seekers creates a fear and perception of a risk of crime”. The Home Office said there was no evidence of increased offending levels in town centres as a result of the people staying there.

‌



Labour accused Reform of fuelling division and dismissed the move as a bid to "waste public money on gesture politics". A party spokeswoman said: “This looks like yet another stunt from Reform – spending £150,000 of taxpayers’ money on a headline-grabbing scheme that their own paper admits gives private guards no more powers than any member of the public.

“People deserve to feel safe in their communities with proper neighbourhood policing and serious action on antisocial behaviour – not by using public money for political theatre. This is what Reform do in power – chase stunts, fuel division and waste public money on gesture politics.”

Liberal Democrat MP for Chelmsford Marie Goldman said: “Instead of stoking division in our community and handing over wads of taxpayer cash to a private security company, Reform UK should be giving the much needed resource to our local police force who are fully trained and have the power to enforce the law.

‌



“We have a system of policing by consent in this country, and the public will be rightly concerned to see Reform handing their money over to an unaccountable private security firm to monitor the area.

"Essex Police are already under funding pressure, and we should be equipping them with the much needed resources to continue doing their job protecting the local community.”

Council leader Peter Harris said the induction process at the site was “woefully inadequate”, especially on the introduction to British culture and “expectations we have of acceptable behaviour toward to women and girls”.

‌



He added: “Concerns for community safety are clearly there, particularly among women and girls, because of the daily gatherings of asylum seekers – gatherings which will increase in number and size as the facility expands.”

The county council said it was in the process of contracting a security company.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

Article continues below

“We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, engaging with local authorities to reduce the impact on communities. And we are reducing the burden on taxpayers, with asylum costs down by over £1 billion since the general election.”

News.title: Woman's jaw drops as Vinted parcel containing wrong item actually has huge value
News.content:
Woman's jaw drops as Vinted parcel containing wrong item actually has huge value

A woman was left gobsmacked when a Vinted parcel that should have contained a Hollister top arrived on her doorstep - but what she received instead has surprising value

View Image The woman was baffled by what arrived in the post (stock photo) (Image: Karl Tapales via Getty Images)

There are few feelings quite like the anticipation of waiting for an online order to arrive. The tracking updates, the knock at the door, the moment you finally get to tear open the packaging, it's all part of the excitement. But for one shopper, that feeling of eager anticipation quickly turned to utter confusion when her delivery turned out to be nothing like what she'd been expecting.

‌



The world of secondhand online shopping has exploded in popularity in recent years. Platforms like Vinted, eBay and Facebook Marketplace have made it easier than ever to snap up pre-loved pieces at a fraction of the original price, but the experience doesn't always go smoothly. Without being able to physically inspect an item before handing over your money, you're placing a considerable amount of trust in a stranger, and sometimes that trust is tested in the most unexpected of ways.

‌



That's exactly what happened to a woman named Jem, who took to TikTok to share a video of herself unboxing a parcel she'd received through Vinted. She had paid for a secondhand Hollister top, which she was planning to take away on an upcoming holiday.

‌



Instead, she pulled out something entirely different, a cuddly toy in the shape of an ear of corn. Although upon closer inspection, it turned out the stuffed toy was actually a Jellycat - a brand of plush toys that collectors love.

She said: "I'm extremely confused. What's happening? This is supposed to be a cute top from Hollister that I was planning to take on holiday when I go on holiday in a few days. This is not a cute top from Hollister, this is a corn Jellycat."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



The toy was a Vivacious Vegetable Sweetcorn, and it has been retired from the Jellycat website. This means the only place to buy them is through secondhand sellers, where they can be priced as much as £30.

Jem's suspicions had first been raised when she opened the plastic postal bag to find a white paper bag inside - not exactly the kind of packaging you'd expect for a clothing item. Her confusion only grew as she dug deeper, and the cuddly toy came into view.

To make matters worse, the timing couldn't have been much worse. With her holiday just days away, Jem found herself without the top she'd been counting on to pack, and with very little time to resolve the situation before she was due to travel. She noted that this kind of mix-up had never happened to her before, and she wasn't entirely sure how best to handle it.

‌



In the caption of her video, she revealed she had "submitted a review" with Vinted in an attempt to get her money back, having clearly not received the item she'd purchased. Whether or not that has led to a resolution remains unclear, as she has yet to share a follow-up video with her followers.

The comments section quickly filled with advice from fellow Vinted users. Many urged Jem to reach out to the seller directly, suggesting the most likely explanation was a simple labelling error - meaning whoever had ordered the Jellycat corn had probably received her Hollister top by mistake.

Others felt she had taken the right approach by going straight to Vinted. Although the platform doesn't directly facilitate sales, it does step in to manage disputes and issue refunds when things go wrong. Buyers are given two days after delivery to check their item and confirm that "everything is okay" - a step that triggers the release of funds to the seller. If something isn't right, buyers can raise a complaint and may be asked to submit photographic evidence, with Vinted staff ultimately determining whether a refund should be issued.

Article continues below

One commenter shared a surprisingly relatable story from the other side of the transaction: "This happened to me as a SELLER! I'm a fool and mixed up two labels. Both buyers were lovely and let me pay for new shipping labels, and both shipped each other their parcels."

Another pointed to a potentially positive sign in Jem's package: "That must have been a mistake! It even has tags."

A third offered a glimpse of what the outcome might look like, drawing on their own similar experience: "You'll get to keep it and get your money back, but the Hollister top is long gone. I was supposed to receive some brand new gym leggings, and instead I got 13 DVDs. I got to keep them and got my money back."

News.title: Everything you're entitled to if airline loses your luggage
News.content:
Everything you're entitled to if airline loses your luggage

Holidaymakers may be entitled to claim compensation when an airline loses, damages or delays their luggage

View 3 Images The compensation available from an airline is generally limited (Image: anyaberkut via Getty Images)

Holidaymakers facing the misery of lost, damaged or delayed luggage could be entitled to compensation from their airline - but they need to act quickly.

‌



Passengers arriving at their destination only to discover their suitcase has failed to make the journey with them have legal rights that can help them recover some of the costs. Citizens Advice says travellers have the right to claim compensation from an airline when checked-in luggage is delayed, lost or damaged. But there are important deadlines - and passengers should report a problem as soon as possible.

‌



The consumer advice charity warns that the rules for cabin baggage are different. You can generally only claim for a problem with hand luggage where the airline was at fault.

‌



Don't leave it too late

Citizens Advice says holidaymakers should report missing or damaged luggage to the airline straight away. At the airport, this will normally involve completing a Property Irregularity Report (PIR) at the baggage claims area.

Passengers should keep a copy of the PIR, or obtain written confirmation from the airline if they report the problem later. Making a report does not necessarily mean a compensation claim has been made. Passengers will normally still need to submit a separate claim unless the airline agrees to pay certain expenses upfront.

View 3 Images holidaymakers should report missing or damaged luggage to the airline straight away (Image: skynesher via Getty Images)

‌



There are strict deadlines

One of the biggest traps is assuming there is plenty of time to make a claim.

Citizens Advice says the usual deadlines are:

Damaged luggage: claim within seven days of receiving it.

Missing or damaged contents: claim within seven days of receiving the luggage.

Delayed or missing luggage: claim within 21 days of the flight.

Luggage not returned within 21 days: it is officially treated as lost, meaning passengers should make a claim as soon as possible.

‌



A suitcase that eventually turns up after several days does not necessarily mean a passenger has lost their right to compensation. Citizens Advice says it is still possible to claim for delayed luggage if it is returned within the 21-day period.

What can you claim for?

The compensation available from an airline is generally limited. For delayed luggage, this can include the cost of essential items needed while waiting for the suitcase, such as toiletries and underwear.

Passengers may also be able to claim some of the cost of repairing or replacing luggage and its contents if they are lost or damaged. If a traveller has to collect delayed luggage themselves, says they may also be able to recover reasonable transport costs.

‌



But holidaymakers should not assume they will receive the full replacement value of everything inside a suitcase. Airlines will often ask for receipts and proof of purchase, while Citizens Advice warns that they will not normally pay 'new for old' replacement costs.

There can also be restrictions around valuable, fragile or perishable items packed in checked luggage. Total compensation is generally limited to around £1,000 and is often considerably less.

Passengers cannot normally claim for stress or inconvenience caused by the luggage problem, or for knock-on problems such as missing a connection.

‌



View 3 Images You can generally only claim for a problem with hand luggage where the airline was at fault (Image: John Nordell via Getty Images)

Keep every scrap of evidence

Anyone making a claim should keep hold of their paperwork.

Citizens Advice says airlines will usually expect passengers to provide documents such as:

‌



their boarding pass;

luggage tags showing the identification number;

the PIR or written confirmation that the problem was reported;

receipts for emergency purchases made because of delayed luggage;

proof of purchase for lost or damaged belongings;

photographs showing damage; and

estimates for the cost of repairs where relevant.

Travellers should keep copies of their claim and the original documents.

How to make the claim

Passengers should check with their airline to find out how it wants compensation claims submitted. If there is no specific claim form, Citizens Advice says travellers may need to write to the airline's customer service department.

‌



The charity advises making clear that the claim is being made under the Montreal Convention. The claim should include details of the flight, including the date, flight number, departure point and destination.

Travellers should explain what happened, set out the amount being claimed and provide a detailed list of the luggage or contents that were lost or damaged. Any essential items bought because of the delay should also be listed, with copies of supporting receipts and other evidence.

What if several airlines were involved?

Passengers travelling on connecting flights operated by different airlines may be able to claim against any of them. However, Citizens Advice says most airlines expect the claim to be made against the last airline boarded.

‌



An airline cannot simply refuse to deal with a claim because another carrier was involved. If a passenger gets nowhere they can seek advice from the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA).

What if the airline rejects your claim?

Holidaymakers who are unhappy with an airline's response can take the matter further. Citizens Advice recommends first trying to resolve the complaint through the appropriate process.

The CAA can take up complaints against airlines or airports in certain circumstances, although its role depends on whether the airline or airport belongs to an approved alternative dispute resolution scheme. As a last resort, passengers can consider taking a case to the small claims court.

‌



A luggage claim can generally be taken to court within two years of the flight, although court action can be costly and time-consuming.

Check your insurance too

There is another option that could prove easier and more generous. Citizens Advice says that if luggage is covered by travel insurance or a home contents policy, making an insurance claim may be preferable.

This is because insurance can potentially provide more money and may be easier to claim through than pursuing the airline.

Article continues below

Passengers needing further help can contact the Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133 or use its online service.

The charity also advises checking the specific rules applying to the airline, as individual procedures and deadlines can vary. More information here.

News.title: Toby Carvery chaos as 'man tasered' and pair arrested over child neglect
News.content:
Toby Carvery chaos as 'man tasered' and pair arrested over child neglect

Police were called to a Toby Carvery in Chadderton in Greater Manchester on Friday evening

View 2 Images (Image: MEN)

Police deployed tasers before two people were arrested in an incident outside of a Toby Carvery restaurant in Chadderton on Friday evening.

‌



Emergency services swarmed the popular restaurant last night (Friday, August 28). It has been reported that a man appeared to have been running from police officers before he was tasered in the car park.

‌



The restaurant, located on Chadderton Park, Oldham, was closed for a short period of time after a number of police cars and an ambulance were spotted outside, witnesses said, Manchester Evening News reports.

‌



View 2 Images (Image: MEN)

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) has today confirmed that a man and a woman have been arrested and remain in custody. Police say that officers noticed a vehicle driving erratically and conducted a vehicle stop at 7.45pm on Friday evening.

‌



After approaching and speaking to the driver, Police say that he became "aggressive", which led the officers to deploy their taser.

Officers searched the vehicle before the man who was driving was arrested on suspicion of assaulting two officers, possession with intent to supply class B, and child neglect. A passenger, a woman, was also arrested on suspicion of child neglect and the pair remain in police custody for questioning.

Greater Manchester Police said in a statement: "At 7.45pm on Friday 28 August, officers conducted a vehicle stop after observing vehicle driving in an erratic manner," a GMP statement reads.

Article continues below

It continues: "Officers spoke to the driver, who then became aggressive and a taser was deployed.

"Following a search of the vehicle, a man was subsequently arrested on suspicion of assaulting two officers, possession with intent to supply class B, and child neglect.

"A woman, a passenger, was also arrested on suspicion of child neglect. They remain in custody for questioning."

News.title: Russian warships task force tracked through UK waters in 'intensive' Royal Navy operation
News.content:
Russian warships task force tracked through UK waters in 'intensive' Royal Navy operation

Several Royal Navy vessels, including a destroyer, were deployed to track a Russian shadow fleet task group as it made its way through the English Channel last week

View 4 Images The Navy undertook a major operation in the English Channel last week (Image: Royal Navy)

The Royal Navy tracked a Russian destroyer and clutch of sanctioned cargo vessels through British waters in an "intense" 72-hour operation.

‌



The Navy said it had deployed the HMS Duncan, a Type 45 destroyer, the Type 23 HMS St Albans and HMS Severn patrol vessel to track the destroyer, Admiral Levchenko, and sanctioned escortees General Skobelev and Sparta. A significant British presence, including the Type 45 destroyer HMS Duncan, Type 23 frigate HMS St Albans and patrol vessel HMS Severn, tracked the task group as it made its way from the North Sea through the English Channel.

‌



It was met with a bristling response from the Russian vessels, with officials saying they deployed additional military resources after the tracking began.

‌



Putin shows off Brit 'traitor' fighting against Ukraine on Russian TV READ MORE :

View 4 Images The Russian vessels were tracked as they neared the Strait of Dover (Image: Royal Navy)

Navy officials said the tracking began when the ships approached the Strait of Dover, to which Russia responded by deploying the Neustrashimy frigate to guard the illegal shipment. They spent the following 72 hours closely observing the task group over the following "intense" 72 hours before the duties were handed over to a Nato ally.

First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continue to pose “an unacceptable risk” to maritime security and the environment.

‌



He said: “Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose. That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required." Tracking was handed off near the French island of Ushant.

View 4 Images The Navy said Russia responded by deploying additional military assistance (Image: Royal Navy)

The operation comes after the Navy warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters earlier this month following 21 days worth of monitoring Moscow's ships in July.

‌



Naval operations to monitor Russian activity increased 25 percent in July compared to the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the Dover Strait and North Sea. Moscow uses its shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.

The increase in Russian naval activity follows the seizure of the tanker Smyrtos by Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.

View 4 Images Tracking duties were handed off to Nato allies after the ships travelled up the Channel (Image: Royal Navy)

‌



It comes after a week of repeated threats from the Kremlin to the UK following Andy Burnham ’s visit to Kyiv, during which he announced Britain would provide Ukraine with blueprints for long-range Scalp missiles. Western officials have sought to play down the prospect of a conflict between Russia and Nato, despite senior figures in Moscow accusing Ukraine’s allies, including the UK, of “playing with fire”.

Ex-Russian foreign minister Andrei Fedorov also said he could not “100% exclude” the possibility of “semi-military” action against Britain in retaliation, raising the prospect of an attack on British drone factories from “unknown sources.”

On Friday, Western officials said the threats were “not a new phenomenon” but part of “long-standing Russian military doctrine” that seeks to use “hostile rhetoric” to “exploit fears” and influence decisions.

Article continues below

“We do need to be careful to distinguish what is real from what is rhetoric designed to scare and deter us. Replaying Russian threats and heightening a sense of crisis is exactly what the Kremlin wants,” they said. “Our assessment remains that Russia isn’t seeking direct confrontation with Nato.”

News.title: Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor
News.content:
Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has said he is resigning from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor.

"I am putting myself forward to be the Conservative candidate for mayor of London, because our capital needs more than an administrator," he wrote in the Times, external.

Sir James said he has told Tory leader Kemi Badenoch he is stepping down as shadow housing secretary, saying: "I must be free to speak about every aspect of London's future and concentrate fully on winning this race."

The capital is not set to vote on a new mayor until May 2028. Labour incumbent Sir Sadiq Khan is yet to confirm whether he will seek an unprecedented fourth term.

The Conservatives are yet to pick their candidate for the London mayoral race.

A source close to Badenoch said Cleverly "is a formidable politician and will out-campaign Khan".

Sir James, who was foreign secretary under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, wrote that he intended to make London a city to be proud of again.

"We must rebuild its reputation and make it, once again, the best place in the world to live, work, invest and build a business," he added.

A senior Conservative politician, Sir James has held a number of ministerial positions under three prime ministers - including roles as home secretary and education secretary.

The army reservist represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.

After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative party leader in 2024, losing out to Badenoch.

Reacting to Sir James's announcement, a source said Badenoch "really didn't want James to leave shadow cabinet", but believed "he will be a big asset in London".

Current London Mayor Sir Sadiq began his first term in 2016. Cleverly wrote that the capital has been "let down by Labour".

He accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of treating London as a "cash cow: somewhere to tax, regulate, raid and blame".

Sir James said: "Londoners need homes they can afford to buy or rent. Entrepreneurs need to be able to start and grow businesses without being strangled by cost and regulation."

The last time Londoners voted for their mayor in May 2024, Sir Sadiq beat Conservative rival Susan Hall by more than 275,000 votes - representing a swing of 3.2% to Labour.

The mayor won nine of the 14 constituencies including two gains from the Tories, and gained 43.8% of the vote share.

Reform UK revealed its candidate for the May 2028 election in January when it announced Westminster City councillor Laila Cunningham would be standing.

Reacting on social media, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage wrote the Conservatives are "done for", and said Cleverly "will not be the first Tory MP to give up any hope of winning their seat in Essex".

Cleverly has not resigned as an MP yet.

His announcement follows speculation in recent weeks that he would step down and launch a bid to become London's next mayor.

During his time at the London Assembly, Cleverly chaired the London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority, and also worked for Boris Johnson while he was mayor of London.

News.title: Mum of Nottingham attacks victim backs calls to stop killers' early release
News.content:
More than 30 families have called on the government to stop killers convicted of any form of manslaughter being released early to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.

In a letter to Justice Secretary Alex Norris, the families said they felt victims were "being asked to bear the consequences of the prison capacity crisis".

Signatories include Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was stabbed to death in the Nottingham attacks in 2023, and whose killer Valdo Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Bridget Phillipson, Minister for Women and Equalities, defended the early release scheme.

She said the government had faced "some really difficult and unpalatable choices" in dealing with prison overcrowding and that they had faced "the wholesale collapse of the criminal justice system".

The scheme, external aims to ease prison overcrowding in England and Wales.

The families of those affected by homicide have called for those convicted of any form of manslaughter to be excluded.

Those convicted of murder and those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences are already excluded from the early release scheme.

News.title: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK 'shortly', source says
News.content:
Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.

It is believed she has been spending her time out of the public eye at an Alpine chalet in Verbier, Switzerland, since leaving Royal Lodge. Her belongings were collected from Mountbatten-Windsor's home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.

She had been keeping a low profile since losing her titles alongside Mountbatten-Windsor after she became mired in the scandal about her connections to Epstein, and faced calls to speak to US authorities after last year's release of millions of documents shed new light on their relationship.

In one email exchange from 2011, she appeared to privately apologise for her public rejection of Epstein, saying: "You have always been a steadfast, generous and supreme friend to me and my family."

A spokesperson for the duchess previously said the email was sent after Epstein had threatened to sue her for defamation - in an effort to convince him not to.

Another email suggested Ferguson took her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.

The emails do not indicate any wrongdoing.

Epstein was also ultimately the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

Ferguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her maiden name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over the scandal.

Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex came back to Britain with their children to begin a new life after six years living in the US.

News.title: Man dies after train hits van on level crossing
News.content:
A man has died after a train hit a van on a railway line.

The incident happened on a crossing in Burscough, West Lancashire, just after 15:00 BST.

British Transport Police (BTP) said a man who was in the van died at the scene, and two passengers on the Wigan Wallgate-Southport train suffered minor injuries.

A BTP spokesman said: "Enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances of what happened."

News.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
News.content:
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.

Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.

The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.

Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.

Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

More on this story here.

News.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
News.content:
New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands more are missing, Nepalese officials say.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

News.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
News.content:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of Â£5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

News.title: We're behind UK's emergency phone alerts - but question how they're being used
News.content:
The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.

It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.

Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales.

"People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."

A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts.

"Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.

The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries.

"By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.

But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.

He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around.

"Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."

His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"

Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life.

"It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.

News.title: Christian festival 'devastated' after man's death
News.content:
Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.

Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.

It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.

The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.

Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them.

"And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.

"May the God of comfort and healing be with them all."

South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.

The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.

The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.

"We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said.

"We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

News.title: Football fans pay tribute to crash death officers
News.content:
Football fans and players have paid tribute to two Cleveland Police officers who were killed in a crash on Teesside.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision between their police car and a vehicle going the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough early on 22 August. Five people in the other vehicle also died.

There was a minute's applause in their memory ahead of Middlesbrough and West Bromwich Albion's Championship match at Riverside Stadium, as pictures of the two men were displayed on a screen.

People also gathered to pay tribute at Seaton Carew FC's game against FC Hartlepool. PC Matthew Blades had been a junior football coach at both teams.

Seaton Carew FC coach Marcus Newing, who was friends with him, said the past week had been "horrendous", but seeing the "outpouring" from the nation had been "comforting".

"People would probably say that he's the goal of a dad and a husband," Newing said.

News.title: Strong winds and thunderstorms kick off the bank holiday weekend
News.content:
After weeks of scorching heat and drought the summer's swan song is set to be one of frequent downpours as well as gales for some.

Areas of heavy rain and showers are expected to sweep across parts of the UK on each day of the weekend, which is a bank holiday for many.

This could make for some soggy moments at many of the festivals taking place over the coming days.

Strong winds and gales may also cause problems for travellers and holidaymakers in southern parts of the UK.

News.title: Royal Navy warships track Russian vessels for three days in UK waters
News.content:
Royal Navy warships and a helicopter spent three days tracking Russian Navy vessels and sanctioned cargo ships in an "intense" operation in the North Sea and English Channel.

HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn used radars to monitor four vessels last week, while a Merlin helicopter provided surveillance from the sky.

"Since that successful operation, we have seen Russian shadow fleet vessels increasingly forced to change their routes, imposing significant cost and delays to their journeys," Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of Naval Staff, said.

It comes as data shows Royal Navy activity to monitor Russian movements is up 25% so far this year compared to 2025.

During the August operation, the Royal Navy warships including a Type 45 destroyer and a Type 23 frigate, tracked Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko as it escorted sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta south through the North Sea and into the English Channel.

The Royal Navy said Russia was "forced" to respond with "costly military resources" including the frigate Neustrashimy.

A statement said a Nato ally then took over monitoring off the coast of France, without specifying the country.

The operation comes after Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in June.

Marines joined by National Crime Agency (NCA) officers, with the support of the RAF, intercepted and boarded the Smyrtos in a six-hour operation - the first of its kind by UK armed forces.
