World.title: After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat Bridget McManus August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Danny Estrin, the lead singer of Perth progressive metal band Voyager, was told he had 12 months to live, soon after the band performed at the 2023 Eurovision Song Contest. Three years and several rounds of chemotherapy later, the father of two daughters, aged five and nine, is still here. “I decided, I’m just going to enjoy the time between chemotherapy sessions as much as I can,” says Estrin, who is also still holding down his day job as an immigration lawyer. “It’s probably diametrically opposed to what a normal terminal cancer patient should be doing but I’m enjoying life as much as I can and filling it with good stuff.” Danny Estrin with a Porsche 928 in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Voyager have just returned from touring the Netherlands and the UK, and Estrin is stoked to be back on home soil feeding his “lifelong addiction” – cars. Having combed the car meets and garages of Western Australia for other enthusiasts, he’s making his television hosting debut with a fresh take on the motoring lifestyle genre, SBS2’s Precious Metal: A Love Story. His first automotive love was a Mercedes-Benz S-Class he spotted as a child in Hamburg, Germany, where he lived until his parents moved to Perth when he was 11. “It was the ultimate luxury,” he says. “It was huge. It was a 5.3-metre Colossus driven by executives. It had the car phone and electric everything, which back in the day was just crazy. It’s like, ‘Oh, someone important must be in that car!’”



Related Article Analysis

Australian TV Is Kitchen Cabinet past its use-by-date? Don’t write it off yet More a “man of letters and music than a man of wrenches and spanners”, Estrin leaves the mechanical side to his qualified mate, metal music fan Will Keogh, who appears on the show. Estrin has lost count of how many cars he has acquired, most of which are sitting in the garages of friends “with big hearts”. His very first, the white 1988 Toyota MR2 AW11 sports car that appeared alongside him on the Eurovision stage, is on display at the Motor Museum of Western Australia. “There’s something about the design and the shape of cars, and the fact that cars are objects of freedom and boundlessness. The steering wheels, the way the interior feels, smells, looks. The design, the headlights,” he says. “And the way that every car has a face: this one looks a bit sad; this one’s smiling, it’s a happy car. For me, styling was always much more important than the engine. I really couldn’t care about it. For me it’s about, ‘Oh, look! This has rear headrests! This has 16 ashtrays’ – as was the case in Germany in the ’80s. As part of this show I’ve explored other people’s reasons for their passion.” Danny Estrin and fellow motoring enthusiast Graeme take a vintage ride in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Throughout the series, Estrin, sporting his signature shiny houndstooth suits, meets people from all walks of life. Their wheels are just as diverse, among them a Morris Mini, a Renault Spider, a Porsche 356, a 1927 Chrysler Silver Wings, two Jaguars, and a Tesla Model 3/Chrysler 300 SRT Custom. There are also a Nissan Cube and two Toyota Landcruisers, one belonging to the series’ sole celebrity guest, former Neighbours actor Dan Paris, featured in the first episode.



Related Article Australian TV It’s been 25 years since Tampa. A documentary aims to show the story behind it isn’t ‘black and white’ “They don’t necessarily need to be the most exciting cars,” says Estrin. “It’s the stories that are the main thing. It could be teacups. It could be anything that’s collectible and has a sentimental value. I really wanted to explore what connects these people to these pieces of metal.” Voyager are off to the US next month to play at the ProgPower USA festival in Atlanta, and will then tour Australia in November, with shows in Perth, Melbourne and Sydney. “I’m still doing chemotherapy but the brakes are on at the moment. Hey! There’s a good car pun!” he says, laughing. “It’s a pretty aggressive form of cancer, unfortunately. It’ll get me sooner or later but, as statistics go, the longer you are alive, the longer you will be alive, hopefully. It’s quite surreal, actually, to think that this show is about to be released after all the turmoil of the last three years.” Precious Metal: A Love Story premieres on Wednesday, September 2, at 8.30pm on SBS2.

World.title: Leah Purcell is renowned for being tough on screen, but it’s what lies beneath that is the secret to her success
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Laughter might not come easily to the characters Leah Purcell plays: taciturn police sergeant Andie Whitford in High Country; fierce but distraught Molly Johnson in The Drover’s Wife; double-crossed undercover cop, now prisoner, Rita Connors in Wentworth. But asked why she thinks audiences have embraced her High Country character, she erupts in raucous and infectious laughter. “Maybe they just like me … everyone fell in love with me!” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Purcell has forged a remarkably varied and successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women battling adversity and hardship. It’s what lies beneath that hard surface that is key to her appeal. Ariadne Sgouros, Leah Purcell and Brendan Cowell in High Country: What Lies Beneath. What Lies Beneath is also the subtitle of the returning season of the mystery thriller High Country, which sees Whitford back in uniform and investigating dark deeds in a small, close-knit town. For those coming in late – no spoilers – High Country evolves around Purcell’s police officer Andie, who is transferred to a picturesque but insular mountain township of Brokenridge to replace retiring cop Sergeant Sam Dyson (Ian McElhinney, the veteran Northern Ireland actor best known as Barristan Selmy in Game of Thrones). It’s a town filled with grievances, suspicion and vendettas and a handful of missing-person cases. Those disappearances dovetail with the discovery of a far-reaching conspiracy involving many of the town’s residents.



Alongside the mystery-thriller element, High Country also dealt with Andie’s new-found connection to her Indigenous ancestry and relationships with partner Helen (Sara Wiseman), teenage daughter Kirra (Pez Warner) and ageing mother (Melissa Jaffer). Related Article Australian TV ‘Oh Jesus’: When Claudia Karvan agreed to go on Australian Story, she didn’t expect this It was filmed in Victoria’s high country, mainly around the township of Jamieson, which is where John Ridley – who created the show with Marcia Gardner – grew up and continues to live. The dramatic mountain landscape is a key element of the show. It also happens to be a region associated with many real-world events, from missing hikers to the cult known as The Family and most recently the notorious fugitive Dezi Freeman. Purcell wears many hats on High Country. In addition to playing the lead, she is an executive producer, which allows her to have input to the script and key production decisions. She is also the cultural consultant, ensuring all protocols are correctly carried out. That haunting voice on the opening soundtrack is hers as well. Leah Purcell with Aaron Pedersen in the first season of High Country, which was a hit in the UK and US. The new season takes up months after the events of the 2024 debut. It kicks off with a double murder on a houseboat, but there are many continuing storylines and characters, most notably Sam Dyson and Andie’s family. Purcell says that many decisions regarding the new, eight-episode series were based on audience feedback. “Everyone fell in love with their relationship,” she says of Andie and Sam.



“We both thoroughly enjoyed working with one another. So we kept [the storyline] open and everyone’s diaries aligned and away we went,” she says. “He’s a great bloke and phenomenal actor and the story lent itself to opening up that relationship. It’s a thriller, so there’s many threads to the story, and it’s a great thread to have him being a part of.” Related Article Streaming Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since Audiences also felt that Andie’s domestic relationships were authentic. “Pez [Warner] reminded me of myself,” says Purcell. “She had no training, comes from Newcastle, is a little go-getter. We all have a great relationship and I think that comes across clearly in the first season.” Andie has now settled into her job and has begun to understand the lay of the land. But she remains very isolated. Work is her life, her family. We only see her wearing her dark blue uniform. “That was all part of trying to show her isolation and what she’s put herself in at home.” The new cast includes Brendan Cowell as a gnarly, surly and possibly shifty detective who has a contemptuous history with Dyson, as well as a troubling personal connection to the victims of the houseboat murder. Purcell has played opposite Cowell on stage, describing him as deep and very smart. She credits Ridley and Gardner for allowing actors to “mould the words to suit their mouths. Brendan is very clever with that shorthand, which suits his character … the abruptness and poeticness around some of his lines.” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Leah Purcell has forged a successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women. Benny Capp



Season two of High Country has a noticeably different palette and setting to the first, which was dictated by the seasons in which the filming took place. “The lakes were down. So you utilise what you’ve got. He [John Ridley] said it’s a great way for any secrets that are hidden in that man-made lake [to be revealed]. When the water goes down, the secrets will rise and that’s what happens.” Where season one was all lush and damp forests, season two is a baked and receding lake (the actual Lake Eildon), a barren mine and the glare of summer. Related Article Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now “We utilised that in the story, the change of landscape,” says Purcell. “The hardness of a mine, the masculinity in this story. It was all a hardened approach to the various landscapes up there. Turn one way and you’ve got lush mountains. Turn and you’ve got a mine shaft. That was all deliberate, just working with the landscape and the time of year we could shoot.” Purcell believes that the success of High Country in the UK and US, where it aired on BBC and Hulu respectively, was due to it breaking the mould of what Australian stories are normally about. Instead of red-hot desert, viewers saw snow, mountains and greenery. But mostly, she says, it was down to the character. “That’s what you want from your leading lady, that the audience falls in love with the character and what she was going through. And it’s a First Nations story, that was something else that makes this different. A woman trying to work out who she is and there happened to be this First Nations connection to Country. “It wasn’t just the landscape; the landscape was talking. A lot of people thought that was a great addition to our cop story.”



Leah Purcell in The Drover’s Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson, which is being turned into a TV series. Brett Boardmen Purcell recently added librettist to her extensive list of credits, having written the opera adaptation of her play, film and novel The Drover’s Wife, which is also being turned into a TV series. The series “is not what people think. It starts with Molly Johnson’s six-times granddaughter in 2020. We’ve flipped it, coming at it from a different perspective. It’s not just the movie in six episodes. We always try to find a different way into those stories.” There’s nothing accidental about Purcell’s confidence and skill as a TV creator. “People have said, ‘Leah you’re so easy to shoot’. Because I understand what they need, what the camera person needs. It’s experience, and time. It’s a talent to be at one with the camera, just me and it. It’s a talent that you learn if you’re aware of it. Some people can be in the industry forever, and it’s not quite their thing, but I’ve had a couple of DOPs come up to me and say you’re so easy to shoot because you understand what the camera is doing.” Related Article Streaming Why the makers of Netflix’s My Brilliant Career tinkered with a classic She recalls one of her first roles on Police Rescue. “It was my training ground. I would sit and watch and understand when the camera was moving or crept in for a close-up. When Steadicam came in, that was magic, that was like dancing. “I love that challenge. Sometimes you can get caught up for a very long time trying to get the take if you don’t understand what they’re trying to achieve with the camera. So I would ask them, what do you need from me? It’s all very clinical, it’s maths when you break it down. It’s our job to make it look natural. I learned very early that the relationship other than [with] your fellow actor is with the camera.”

World.title: A black Swan event raises the question no one asks
World.content:
I have read tens of thousands of words over the past fortnight about the Sydney Swans’ debacle at Melbourne’s Pullman hotel, which has dismantled their season and left the club in crisis. There have been an extraordinary number of permutations and opinions, but one question seems still untouched.

To their credit, the Swans hierarchy has expressed the right priorities – decency, the wellbeing of the women involved, responsibility to the wider club and players. But while police and AFL investigations go on separately, the “Pullman five” have been suspended for the rest of the season by the club because they “breached club standards”. My question is, what precisely are these standards?

The misdoings of five suspended Sydney footballers at the Pullman Hotel raise questions about what exactly “club standards” are. Simon Schluter

At what point did the players breach these standards? When they went out partying all night? When they requested lap dances? Or only when they (allegedly) crossed the line into sexual assault?

The problem is that such moral codes are often highly amorphous and deliberately general. While I don’t doubt that the Swans are genuine in wanting high standards – particularly as the sense of betrayal within the club seems so powerful – such codes also provide a shelter behind which to hide in crises like this.

World.title: From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit
World.content:
CultureTV & radioDisney From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit Michael Idato August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Meet the content stream of the future: movies, TV shows and a raft of next-generation spin-offs, coming to a mobile phone near you. While it’s true that bricks-and-mortar cinemas are going nowhere anytime soon, there is one inescapable truth dawning on Hollywood: the future is vertical. YouTube calls them Shorts, Netflix calls them Clips and on Disney+ they are Verts: a bite-sized, swipe-able TikTok-style feed of short-form content, including trailers, typically aimed at upsizing you to the full movie or episode. Loading But following a new deal with TikTok, Disney’s Verts are expanding into fan-created content and, coupled with a suite of spin-offs pitched at younger audiences, including Ariel, The Lion Guard, Star Wars: Young Jedi Adventures and Descendants: The Rise of Red, represent the studio’s most significant shift towards younger viewers in decades. Critics might see this as the TikTok-ification of content, in the midst of the YouTube-ification of platforms: shrinking everything to the mobile phone, both in size and scale of ambition. Indeed, under the new deal, fan-created content would be seen on TikTok and inside the Disney+ app. That’s a substantial step past running trailers and preview clips.



But Shorts, Clips and Verts, and their longer form cousin, the “vertical drama”, may not be the cinematic death knell their critics might fear them to be. The key detail: 2026 has also been an extraordinary year for bricks-and-mortar cinemas. Despite fears streaming would destroy movie houses, global ticket sales are up 15 per cent year-on-year, and five films have crossed the $US1 billion mark this year in global box office receipts. Disney chief executive Josh D’Amaro on the main stage at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images They are Michael, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie and Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, from Universal Pictures, and Toy Story 5 and Spider-Man: Brand New Day, from Disney’s Marvel Studios and Sony. Two more films – The Devil Wears Prada 2 (Disney) and Project Hail Mary (Amazon MGM and Sony) – are just shy of the $US700 million mark, and Disney has another monster hit due before the end of the year, Avengers: Doomsday, in December.



The Disney+ Verts screen. So what is going on? And why, when cinema is upsizing to IMAX for The Odyssey, is consumable content in the home downsizing? The answer may be generational, as companies like Disney sharpen their aim at new, younger audiences. Earlier this month, as tens of thousands of fans moved through the D23 convention in Anaheim, California, showing off cosplay costumes, buying merchandise and engaging with the studio’s brand “activations”, behind closed doors its executives were outlining the future of the studio’s content strategy. And central to that strategy, says Erin Teague, Disney’s executive vice-president of product management for Disney Entertainment and ESPN, is the “democratisation of creativity.” “Next generations of fans are expecting more from their entertainment experience,” Teague told media in the closed-door press meeting. “They want to be a part of the story. They want to put themselves in the story. They want interactivity. They want to have more agency in the storytelling experience.”



Disney’s strategy includes a $US1.5 billion investment in Epic Games, which essentially lays down digital bedrock for gamers to engage with Disney IP – Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars and more – inside the Fortnite gameplay environment. In addition to the studio’s suite of next-generation spin-offs, variously about younger versions of known characters (Ariel, Marvel’s Iron Man and his Awesome Friends) or siblings and offspring (The Lion Guard, Descendants: The Rise of Red), a substantial new slate for Pixar was unveiled at D23. Ginnifer Goodwin and Ke Huy Quan unveil The Bluey Movie at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images That included Incredibles 3, Coco 2 and Frozen 3, on top of original films Gatto, about a street-smart black cat, due out in 2027, and Ghost Market, Pixar’s first supernatural thriller, due out in 2028. There is also, separately, a Bluey movie. There’s a good reason for that. As much as rusted-on fans might not like to hear it, key pieces of the Disney ecosystem are showing their age. Star Wars, the home of Luke Skywalker and Princess Leia, turns 50 next year. Marvel’s Cinematic Universe is in phase six, almost two decades after phase one began. Even Thor is starting to look a little long in the hammer.



Another perspective Disney The A-list stars added to Disney’s hall of fame – and what that means for the studio’s future Along with vertical content, however, all roads ultimately lead back to the central content funnel, Disney+. In the past two years the studio has consolidated its assets under the brand, including Hulu, its US-streamer, which is now tucked inside the Australian Disney+ app, and its sports streaming app, ESPN. Eric Schrier, the president of Disney Television Studios, said the strategy was intended to join dots for new audiences, who have not watched older, institutional content such as The Simpsons, Star Wars or even Disney live-action films, but might sample them via the streamer’s vertical and other content. “It gives us an opportunity to take a generation that is consuming most of this content in short form and introducing them to something like The Simpsons,” Schrier told the D23 press briefing. “They may not watch the traditional Simpsons show. They may see clips online, they may see curation, and then eventually become fans of The Simpsons and watch the whole show completely.” And all of this comes as Hollywood obsesses about vertical dramas, the phone-sized, modestly budgeted soap operas which have effectively turned handbags into home entertainment consoles.



Last month, Atlanta hosted the first vertical film festival, Vertex Micro Fest, which focused on short-form vertical content, “micro-dramas” and “AI-powered” stories, while Los Angeles last week hosted Verticon, a fan convention where fans and vertical drama stars pressed the flesh for three days. Verticon also played host to the Verties, the vertical content world’s answer to the Emmys or Oscars. The best actor and actress awards went to Cayman Cardiff (Seducing My Hockey Rival) and Nicole Mattox (Found a Homeless Billionaire Husband for Christmas); vertical of the year was the romantic thriller Swipe Left: Dying for Love, from indie studio muVpix. Discussing Disney’s future: Content creator Blake Silva, Disney executives Eric Schrier and Erin Teague, and moderator (and creator) Jon Youshaei. The Walt Disney Company/Image Group L.A. Setting aside the eyebrow-raising titles, the vertical content business is now worth about $US150 billion globally; vertical dramas account for about $US14 billion of that. At Disney, the vertical strategy was initially tested as a sidebar product within the company’s ESPN ecosystem, before being rolled out widely. What testing in sport revealed, Teague said, was that time-challenged consumers were seeking a way of engaging with the major hits.



Editor's pick Film & TV production The palm-of-your-hand soap operas turning viewers away from TV “There’s no replacement for the live sports viewing experience, but ... thinking about the different ways people are busy, there’s a fight for attention,” Teague said. “People are consuming the live content, but they’re also catching up with key plays, with highlights, and all of that content is short, and actually better natively for a mobile consumption experience,” she said. Teague said viewer engagement had doubled since Verts were launched. In the end, however, replacing legacy IP with enduring appeal will be tough. Disney’s vertical content play can map the Star Wars universe infinitely outward, but few characters can match Princess Leia or Darth Vader for audience recognition, engagement and loyalty. “There will never be a replacement for that long-form original content,” Teague said. “But what is interesting is the way that it is now being supplemented by the shorter form analysis, the clips. Similarly, [in sport] there’s no replacement for the live game. But the additional commentary and analysis around the game is just as interesting.



“The ways that we can merge those experiences to give people exactly what they want, when they want it in a split second, is the challenge.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Clinging to hope: Relatives of missing Sydney family arrive in Nepal
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods Clinging to hope: Relatives of missing Sydney family arrive in Nepal Bishal Karki Zach Hope and August 30, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bidur, Nepal: Relatives of a missing Australian family have arrived in remote Nepal in the desperate hope of finding their loved ones among the survivors rescued from last Wednesday’s deadly floods. The four brothers spoke to this masthead from an army camp at the Nepalese town of Bidur, as helicopters - often carrying injured or shaken survivors - landed roughly every 10 minutes from obliterated regions upstream. Kishore Ramaswamy (left) and Karthik Venkatachalam (right) arrive in a remote part of Nepal to search for their brother Sreedharan Iyer and his family. KATE GERAGHTY Missing is their eldest brother, Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife Lakshmi, 49, and the couple’s two sons, Rudhra, 20, and Rishab, 23. The family, from the Sydney suburb of Cherrybrook, was travelling with a group of about 15 Australian friends to the Hindu sacred site of Mount Kailash when an ice avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border sent water surging downstream, wiping out villages and leaving more than 2000 people dead or missing.



“Not a single person, be it from the embassy, army or rescue team operations have been able to give us a lead concrete enough to say, ‘my family is there’,” Ganesh Gopalakrishnan said on Saturday. “[But] they have been very helpful. And we have positivity.” The two Sydney brothers Rudhra Iyer and Rishab Iyer were travelling with their parents when the disaster struck. Ganesh was at work in Bangalore when he first learned the shocking news that a disaster was unfolding exactly where his family members were travelling. “We didn’t have the itinerary with us so we had to start from scratch, starting with the tour operator,” he said.



“From there we found the itinerary and the place they spent that last night and morning, and then when they would have checked out. That was 8.45am.” Related Article Floods ‘I must look for my sons’: A farmer’s extraordinary survival in Nepal The timeline meant the tour group was leaving the Hotel Kalaish only minutes after the avalanche upstream. “They were on their way towards the border check post [to get to Mount Kalaish],” Ganesh said. “It could have been they were face to face with the floods coming at them, and we just hope they managed to park their cars and escape to an elevated area.” None of the 52 people on the tour, which includes 35 Australians, have been found. Nor has any of the 11 vehicles they were travelling in.



The combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 676 on Saturday, but it is likely to rise sharply because almost 3000 people, including 41 Australians, are still missing. Loading More than 3700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Lakshmi runs the Leap Pad Early Learning Centre in Riverstone, the brothers said. Sreedharan is a mortgage broker. Their eldest son, Rishab, is a doctor, while Rudhra is studying medicine at a university in Sydney. “It is [Sreedharan’s] dream to get his children to become doctors,” Ganesh said. “He’s been very successful in getting two fine boys.”

World.title: How can we invest for our grandkids when markets are so volatile?
World.content:
August 30, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Currently, I have investment bonds for my grandchildren invested in a high-growth option, given the money will sit in their for a long time. With the arrival of a new child, and perceived increased uncertainty in the market, is this still the way forward? Should I now be taking a more conservative approach? In a word, no. There is always market noise, and if we look for it, a reason to convince ourselves to sit on the side lines. Markets today are no more uncertain than they were last year, or 10 years ago. They will rise around 4 out of 5 years. Negative years will happen, and are part of investing. Volatile markets are part and parcel of any long-term investment strategy. Simon Letch The higher returns you receive from stock market investments is the compensation you get for tolerating occasional negative returns. This investment for your new grandchild will likely run 20 years plus. Over that time span the positive years will significantly outweigh the negative. Your current strategy is a good one, stick to it.



My wife and I are in our 70s and have a self-managed super fund in pension mode. We find the fees are becoming prohibitive. We would like to sell our portfolio and join an industry fund. Would you have any advice on how to transition over, as we are not confident in selling our fund? Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Should I sell my $1m investment property and put it into my super? Noel Whittaker Money columnist You are on the right track with regards the process. First, you would each open accounts with your super fund of choice. Next you would liquidate the assets in the SMSF. If it is a share portfolio you could have your cash in three days. Property assets will take longer, and if you have term deposits, you may need to wait for them to mature. Where you want to get to, is having your total SMSF balance held in cash. You would then work in concert with your fund’s accountant to get the monies rolled over from the SMSF to your new accounts via the SuperStream system. It is crucial to get this step right. Do not try and DIY this element.



It needs to be a rollover rather than a withdrawal. Done incorrectly you could have contribution cap and potentially transfer balance cap problems. Typically, you’d leave a few thousand dollars behind in the SMSF to cover wind-up costs. With regard to having the confidence to pull the trigger on this, perhaps you could lean on the fund’s accountant, or the financial planner who assists you with the SMSF. My mother, aged 90, is of sound mind and lives independently on her own and in her own home. She receives a defined benefit pension of $55,000 pa. She needs another $25,000 pa to cover all her living expenses. She recently sold an investment property and netted $1.4 million which is currently invested in term deposits. She is interested in very low-risk investments with a minimum of administration. Are there alternate investment options or structures that would reduce tax liabilities relative to term deposits? Thanks for your question. From what you describe the term deposits seem like a pretty good fit here. Her tax liability would be negligible. She could use insurance bonds, however these pay tax within the bond at 30 per cent, which would almost certainly be higher than the rate of tax your mother would pay. The term deposit interest will be more than she needs for her $25,000 per year income shortfall, so she could reinvest the surplus to help her investment sum maintain its purchasing power.



Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Financial Services. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. Questions to: paul@financialautonomy.com.au Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Victor spent three nights waiting in a Sydney ED. He left without finishing his treatment
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare Victor spent three nights waiting in a Sydney ED. He left without finishing his treatment Rachel Rasker August 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victor Ishak spent three nights waiting in Bankstown’s emergency department with his left leg swelled to almost double its size, and barely able to walk. The 70-year-old was sent to the ED by his GP, who immediately saw the potential red flags. He spent last Friday night on a hard chair in the hospital’s public reception area, as other patients slept on the floor, then the next two nights on a chair that reclined – but not enough to sleep. Victor Ishak spent three nights in Bankstown’s emergency department. George Chan “It was like a halfway house,” Ishak said. “We’re not in a Third World country, we shouldn’t be in systems like this.” By Monday evening – his fourth night in the ED – Ishak was told there were simply not enough beds: “They gave us all an option to either stay where we were in those chairs, or to go home.”



Ishak said although his ankle still resembled “a baby elephant” he chose to sleep in the comfort of his own bed. He returned the next day to see a specialist, with Liverpool Hospital to contact him about taking a sample from his leg. Liverpool did not contact him until Thursday, after this masthead had contacted NSW Health media. Ishak was discharged with no improvement to his swelling. George Chan According to his discharge summary, Ishak was still awaiting the results of 21 tests when he left the hospital. Australian Medical Association NSW president Dr Fred Betros said in an ideal world Ishak would not have been discharged before physicians had received results. “Sometimes it’s an error not to ask for a test, but I think it’s a bigger error to ask for a test and then not know the result before you decide to send someone home.”



In a statement, South Western Sydney LHD apologised to Ishak, and said they were providing follow-up care and support. “During busy periods, some patients may experience longer than expected time in the emergency department while seriously unwell patients are prioritised for emergency care,” the statement read. “We acknowledge it is difficult and frustrating for people when they wait for longer than they expect … and we thank the community for their patience.” Victor Ishak called Bankstown’s ED a “circus”. George Chan Patients across the state are waiting for increasingly prolonged periods, particularly in Sydney’s outer suburbs.



One in 10 patients across NSW waited more than 24 hours to be treated and admitted to a ward or transferred to another hospital in the first quarter of 2026, according to NSW Bureau of Health Information data. That wait time has jumped more than two-and-a-half hours compared to the same period last year. In south-western Sydney, one in 10 patients waited over 28 hours to be admitted, while 10 per cent of Bankstown patients waited about 27 hours. In a bid to address the escalating crisis, the NSW government announced a $130 million investment in a further 22 short-stay recliner chairs at emergency wards across NSW on Monday. These spaces are only intended to house patients for between four and 24 hours. While he acknowledged the privacy of the recliner was more comfortable than the reception area, Ishak spent over 77 hours in Bankstown’s emergency department, and was never offered a bed. Dr Rachael Gill, the NSW branch chair of the Australian College of Emergency Medicine, said it was clear no inpatient beds were available.



“Short stay would not have met this person’s need,” she said, “which is why we’re advocating for an expansion of inpatient capacity [to relieve pressure on emergency]”. Related Article Hospitals The billion-dollar Sydney hospital that’s performing worse than ever Betros agreed, and said while short stay units served a purpose, they were a “Band-Aid solution”. “The long-term solution is having a hospital process that is set up to deal with the patient completely, from the front door all the way to the exit,” he said. “That means getting them into the wards, getting them into their beds, getting their appropriate treatment, and then having the ability to discharge them in a timely manner.”



The NSW government has long blamed clogged hospitals on the Commonwealth, due to the influx of elderly and disabled patients who are medically well enough to be discharged, but who are awaiting a federally funded NDIS or aged care bed. Just 802 new residential aged care places were added in 2024-25, compared to an average of 1800 per year in the previous four financial years. By the federal government’s own projections, Australia needs about 10,600 beds per year to keep up with current demand. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said there were almost 1100 patients waiting in a NSW hospital for an aged care bed, a figure which has almost doubled over the past year. He said the state government was investing $35.7 million in interim services to help older people transition safely out of hospital while awaiting placement or home supports, which would free up the equivalent of about 180 beds per year. Federal Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said the Albanese government has made record investments in the residential aged care and home care system, including $2 billion in the year’s budget to support 5000 more aged care beds each year. Rae said he would continue working with states and territories to ensure older Australians aren’t stuck in hospital.



Eight days waiting for test results Patients at the heart of the crisis say delays in testing are another part of the story. Michael Hirschhorn presented at Westmead’s emergency department with a suspected foot infection on a Wednesday evening in February, and was given a bed the next day. He said a doctor ordered an MRI of his foot on Thursday at noon, but it was not performed until Monday. “Apparently, they don’t do it over the weekend.” Michael Hirschhorn said he took up a bed unnecessarily at Westmead while awaiting MRI results. Janie Barrett He did not receive his results until the following Thursday, a week after his MRI was initially ordered, eight days since he initially presented to hospital. Hirschhorn’s result was negative, and he was discharged that evening.



“I was blocking a bed … just waiting for someone to read the MRI,” he said, with his only other treatment a daily antibiotic. “That bed could have been occupied by someone in a more serious situation.” A doctor at Westmead ED not authorised to speak publicly expressed frustration at what they called a “dysfunctional” hospital, with 20 or 30 people taking up beds at any one time while waiting for results. The doctor said despite being a major hospital, Westmead’s MRI service only operates on weekdays, with results outsourced to an external company in Melbourne, leaving already strained hospital staff to chase up delayed reports. “The other day I discharged a patient to get an MRI as an outpatient, because that would be quicker than getting an MRI at Westmead,” the doctor said.



Gill said healthcare should be considered a seven day a week necessity. “Because the community doesn’t choose when they’re unwell and when they need to access healthcare.” In a statement, Western Sydney Local Health District said MRIs are prioritised according to clinical urgency, while their CT and X-ray services are available 24/7. The spokesperson said NSW Health is currently assessing opportunities to improve equitable access to imaging services across the state. World.title: After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV After Eurovision, Danny Estrin was told he had terminal cancer. He’s now back in the driver’s seat Bridget McManus August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Danny Estrin, the lead singer of Perth progressive metal band Voyager, was told he had 12 months to live, soon after the band performed at the 2023 Eurovision Song Contest. Three years and several rounds of chemotherapy later, the father of two daughters, aged five and nine, is still here. “I decided, I’m just going to enjoy the time between chemotherapy sessions as much as I can,” says Estrin, who is also still holding down his day job as an immigration lawyer. “It’s probably diametrically opposed to what a normal terminal cancer patient should be doing but I’m enjoying life as much as I can and filling it with good stuff.” Danny Estrin with a Porsche 928 in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Voyager have just returned from touring the Netherlands and the UK, and Estrin is stoked to be back on home soil feeding his “lifelong addiction” – cars. Having combed the car meets and garages of Western Australia for other enthusiasts, he’s making his television hosting debut with a fresh take on the motoring lifestyle genre, SBS2’s Precious Metal: A Love Story. His first automotive love was a Mercedes-Benz S-Class he spotted as a child in Hamburg, Germany, where he lived until his parents moved to Perth when he was 11. “It was the ultimate luxury,” he says. “It was huge. It was a 5.3-metre Colossus driven by executives. It had the car phone and electric everything, which back in the day was just crazy. It’s like, ‘Oh, someone important must be in that car!’”



Related Article Analysis

Australian TV Is Kitchen Cabinet past its use-by-date? Don’t write it off yet More a “man of letters and music than a man of wrenches and spanners”, Estrin leaves the mechanical side to his qualified mate, metal music fan Will Keogh, who appears on the show. Estrin has lost count of how many cars he has acquired, most of which are sitting in the garages of friends “with big hearts”. His very first, the white 1988 Toyota MR2 AW11 sports car that appeared alongside him on the Eurovision stage, is on display at the Motor Museum of Western Australia. “There’s something about the design and the shape of cars, and the fact that cars are objects of freedom and boundlessness. The steering wheels, the way the interior feels, smells, looks. The design, the headlights,” he says. “And the way that every car has a face: this one looks a bit sad; this one’s smiling, it’s a happy car. For me, styling was always much more important than the engine. I really couldn’t care about it. For me it’s about, ‘Oh, look! This has rear headrests! This has 16 ashtrays’ – as was the case in Germany in the ’80s. As part of this show I’ve explored other people’s reasons for their passion.” Danny Estrin and fellow motoring enthusiast Graeme take a vintage ride in Precious Metal: A Love Story. Throughout the series, Estrin, sporting his signature shiny houndstooth suits, meets people from all walks of life. Their wheels are just as diverse, among them a Morris Mini, a Renault Spider, a Porsche 356, a 1927 Chrysler Silver Wings, two Jaguars, and a Tesla Model 3/Chrysler 300 SRT Custom. There are also a Nissan Cube and two Toyota Landcruisers, one belonging to the series’ sole celebrity guest, former Neighbours actor Dan Paris, featured in the first episode.



Related Article Australian TV It’s been 25 years since Tampa. A documentary aims to show the story behind it isn’t ‘black and white’ “They don’t necessarily need to be the most exciting cars,” says Estrin. “It’s the stories that are the main thing. It could be teacups. It could be anything that’s collectible and has a sentimental value. I really wanted to explore what connects these people to these pieces of metal.” Voyager are off to the US next month to play at the ProgPower USA festival in Atlanta, and will then tour Australia in November, with shows in Perth, Melbourne and Sydney. “I’m still doing chemotherapy but the brakes are on at the moment. Hey! There’s a good car pun!” he says, laughing. “It’s a pretty aggressive form of cancer, unfortunately. It’ll get me sooner or later but, as statistics go, the longer you are alive, the longer you will be alive, hopefully. It’s quite surreal, actually, to think that this show is about to be released after all the turmoil of the last three years.” Precious Metal: A Love Story premieres on Wednesday, September 2, at 8.30pm on SBS2.

World.title: Leah Purcell is renowned for being tough on screen, but it’s what lies beneath that is the secret to her success
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Laughter might not come easily to the characters Leah Purcell plays: taciturn police sergeant Andie Whitford in High Country; fierce but distraught Molly Johnson in The Drover’s Wife; double-crossed undercover cop, now prisoner, Rita Connors in Wentworth. But asked why she thinks audiences have embraced her High Country character, she erupts in raucous and infectious laughter. “Maybe they just like me … everyone fell in love with me!” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Purcell has forged a remarkably varied and successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women battling adversity and hardship. It’s what lies beneath that hard surface that is key to her appeal. Ariadne Sgouros, Leah Purcell and Brendan Cowell in High Country: What Lies Beneath. What Lies Beneath is also the subtitle of the returning season of the mystery thriller High Country, which sees Whitford back in uniform and investigating dark deeds in a small, close-knit town. For those coming in late – no spoilers – High Country evolves around Purcell’s police officer Andie, who is transferred to a picturesque but insular mountain township of Brokenridge to replace retiring cop Sergeant Sam Dyson (Ian McElhinney, the veteran Northern Ireland actor best known as Barristan Selmy in Game of Thrones). It’s a town filled with grievances, suspicion and vendettas and a handful of missing-person cases. Those disappearances dovetail with the discovery of a far-reaching conspiracy involving many of the town’s residents.



Alongside the mystery-thriller element, High Country also dealt with Andie’s new-found connection to her Indigenous ancestry and relationships with partner Helen (Sara Wiseman), teenage daughter Kirra (Pez Warner) and ageing mother (Melissa Jaffer). Related Article Australian TV ‘Oh Jesus’: When Claudia Karvan agreed to go on Australian Story, she didn’t expect this It was filmed in Victoria’s high country, mainly around the township of Jamieson, which is where John Ridley – who created the show with Marcia Gardner – grew up and continues to live. The dramatic mountain landscape is a key element of the show. It also happens to be a region associated with many real-world events, from missing hikers to the cult known as The Family and most recently the notorious fugitive Dezi Freeman. Purcell wears many hats on High Country. In addition to playing the lead, she is an executive producer, which allows her to have input to the script and key production decisions. She is also the cultural consultant, ensuring all protocols are correctly carried out. That haunting voice on the opening soundtrack is hers as well. Leah Purcell with Aaron Pedersen in the first season of High Country, which was a hit in the UK and US. The new season takes up months after the events of the 2024 debut. It kicks off with a double murder on a houseboat, but there are many continuing storylines and characters, most notably Sam Dyson and Andie’s family. Purcell says that many decisions regarding the new, eight-episode series were based on audience feedback. “Everyone fell in love with their relationship,” she says of Andie and Sam.



“We both thoroughly enjoyed working with one another. So we kept [the storyline] open and everyone’s diaries aligned and away we went,” she says. “He’s a great bloke and phenomenal actor and the story lent itself to opening up that relationship. It’s a thriller, so there’s many threads to the story, and it’s a great thread to have him being a part of.” Related Article Streaming Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since Audiences also felt that Andie’s domestic relationships were authentic. “Pez [Warner] reminded me of myself,” says Purcell. “She had no training, comes from Newcastle, is a little go-getter. We all have a great relationship and I think that comes across clearly in the first season.” Andie has now settled into her job and has begun to understand the lay of the land. But she remains very isolated. Work is her life, her family. We only see her wearing her dark blue uniform. “That was all part of trying to show her isolation and what she’s put herself in at home.” The new cast includes Brendan Cowell as a gnarly, surly and possibly shifty detective who has a contemptuous history with Dyson, as well as a troubling personal connection to the victims of the houseboat murder. Purcell has played opposite Cowell on stage, describing him as deep and very smart. She credits Ridley and Gardner for allowing actors to “mould the words to suit their mouths. Brendan is very clever with that shorthand, which suits his character … the abruptness and poeticness around some of his lines.” As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Leah Purcell has forged a successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women. Benny Capp



Season two of High Country has a noticeably different palette and setting to the first, which was dictated by the seasons in which the filming took place. “The lakes were down. So you utilise what you’ve got. He [John Ridley] said it’s a great way for any secrets that are hidden in that man-made lake [to be revealed]. When the water goes down, the secrets will rise and that’s what happens.” Where season one was all lush and damp forests, season two is a baked and receding lake (the actual Lake Eildon), a barren mine and the glare of summer. Related Article Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on Binge right now “We utilised that in the story, the change of landscape,” says Purcell. “The hardness of a mine, the masculinity in this story. It was all a hardened approach to the various landscapes up there. Turn one way and you’ve got lush mountains. Turn and you’ve got a mine shaft. That was all deliberate, just working with the landscape and the time of year we could shoot.” Purcell believes that the success of High Country in the UK and US, where it aired on BBC and Hulu respectively, was due to it breaking the mould of what Australian stories are normally about. Instead of red-hot desert, viewers saw snow, mountains and greenery. But mostly, she says, it was down to the character. “That’s what you want from your leading lady, that the audience falls in love with the character and what she was going through. And it’s a First Nations story, that was something else that makes this different. A woman trying to work out who she is and there happened to be this First Nations connection to Country. “It wasn’t just the landscape; the landscape was talking. A lot of people thought that was a great addition to our cop story.”



Leah Purcell in The Drover’s Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson, which is being turned into a TV series. Brett Boardmen Purcell recently added librettist to her extensive list of credits, having written the opera adaptation of her play, film and novel The Drover’s Wife, which is also being turned into a TV series. The series “is not what people think. It starts with Molly Johnson’s six-times granddaughter in 2020. We’ve flipped it, coming at it from a different perspective. It’s not just the movie in six episodes. We always try to find a different way into those stories.” There’s nothing accidental about Purcell’s confidence and skill as a TV creator. “People have said, ‘Leah you’re so easy to shoot’. Because I understand what they need, what the camera person needs. It’s experience, and time. It’s a talent to be at one with the camera, just me and it. It’s a talent that you learn if you’re aware of it. Some people can be in the industry forever, and it’s not quite their thing, but I’ve had a couple of DOPs come up to me and say you’re so easy to shoot because you understand what the camera is doing.” Related Article Streaming Why the makers of Netflix’s My Brilliant Career tinkered with a classic She recalls one of her first roles on Police Rescue. “It was my training ground. I would sit and watch and understand when the camera was moving or crept in for a close-up. When Steadicam came in, that was magic, that was like dancing. “I love that challenge. Sometimes you can get caught up for a very long time trying to get the take if you don’t understand what they’re trying to achieve with the camera. So I would ask them, what do you need from me? It’s all very clinical, it’s maths when you break it down. It’s our job to make it look natural. I learned very early that the relationship other than [with] your fellow actor is with the camera.”

World.title: A black Swan event raises the question no one asks
World.content:
I have read tens of thousands of words over the past fortnight about the Sydney Swans’ debacle at Melbourne’s Pullman hotel, which has dismantled their season and left the club in crisis. There have been an extraordinary number of permutations and opinions, but one question seems still untouched.

To their credit, the Swans hierarchy has expressed the right priorities – decency, the wellbeing of the women involved, responsibility to the wider club and players. But while police and AFL investigations go on separately, the “Pullman five” have been suspended for the rest of the season by the club because they “breached club standards”. My question is, what precisely are these standards?

The misdoings of five suspended Sydney footballers at the Pullman Hotel raise questions about what exactly “club standards” are. Simon Schluter

At what point did the players breach these standards? When they went out partying all night? When they requested lap dances? Or only when they (allegedly) crossed the line into sexual assault?

The problem is that such moral codes are often highly amorphous and deliberately general. While I don’t doubt that the Swans are genuine in wanting high standards – particularly as the sense of betrayal within the club seems so powerful – such codes also provide a shelter behind which to hide in crises like this.

World.title: From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit
World.content:
CultureTV & radioDisney From the big screen to your mobile: Inside Disney’s Gen Z gambit Michael Idato August 30, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Meet the content stream of the future: movies, TV shows and a raft of next-generation spin-offs, coming to a mobile phone near you. While it’s true that bricks-and-mortar cinemas are going nowhere anytime soon, there is one inescapable truth dawning on Hollywood: the future is vertical. YouTube calls them Shorts, Netflix calls them Clips and on Disney+ they are Verts: a bite-sized, swipe-able TikTok-style feed of short-form content, including trailers, typically aimed at upsizing you to the full movie or episode. Loading But following a new deal with TikTok, Disney’s Verts are expanding into fan-created content and, coupled with a suite of spin-offs pitched at younger audiences, including Ariel, The Lion Guard, Star Wars: Young Jedi Adventures and Descendants: The Rise of Red, represent the studio’s most significant shift towards younger viewers in decades. Critics might see this as the TikTok-ification of content, in the midst of the YouTube-ification of platforms: shrinking everything to the mobile phone, both in size and scale of ambition. Indeed, under the new deal, fan-created content would be seen on TikTok and inside the Disney+ app. That’s a substantial step past running trailers and preview clips.



But Shorts, Clips and Verts, and their longer form cousin, the “vertical drama”, may not be the cinematic death knell their critics might fear them to be. The key detail: 2026 has also been an extraordinary year for bricks-and-mortar cinemas. Despite fears streaming would destroy movie houses, global ticket sales are up 15 per cent year-on-year, and five films have crossed the $US1 billion mark this year in global box office receipts. Disney chief executive Josh D’Amaro on the main stage at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images They are Michael, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie and Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, from Universal Pictures, and Toy Story 5 and Spider-Man: Brand New Day, from Disney’s Marvel Studios and Sony. Two more films – The Devil Wears Prada 2 (Disney) and Project Hail Mary (Amazon MGM and Sony) – are just shy of the $US700 million mark, and Disney has another monster hit due before the end of the year, Avengers: Doomsday, in December.



The Disney+ Verts screen. So what is going on? And why, when cinema is upsizing to IMAX for The Odyssey, is consumable content in the home downsizing? The answer may be generational, as companies like Disney sharpen their aim at new, younger audiences. Earlier this month, as tens of thousands of fans moved through the D23 convention in Anaheim, California, showing off cosplay costumes, buying merchandise and engaging with the studio’s brand “activations”, behind closed doors its executives were outlining the future of the studio’s content strategy. And central to that strategy, says Erin Teague, Disney’s executive vice-president of product management for Disney Entertainment and ESPN, is the “democratisation of creativity.” “Next generations of fans are expecting more from their entertainment experience,” Teague told media in the closed-door press meeting. “They want to be a part of the story. They want to put themselves in the story. They want interactivity. They want to have more agency in the storytelling experience.”



Disney’s strategy includes a $US1.5 billion investment in Epic Games, which essentially lays down digital bedrock for gamers to engage with Disney IP – Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars and more – inside the Fortnite gameplay environment. In addition to the studio’s suite of next-generation spin-offs, variously about younger versions of known characters (Ariel, Marvel’s Iron Man and his Awesome Friends) or siblings and offspring (The Lion Guard, Descendants: The Rise of Red), a substantial new slate for Pixar was unveiled at D23. Ginnifer Goodwin and Ke Huy Quan unveil The Bluey Movie at D23. Jesse Grant/Getty Images That included Incredibles 3, Coco 2 and Frozen 3, on top of original films Gatto, about a street-smart black cat, due out in 2027, and Ghost Market, Pixar’s first supernatural thriller, due out in 2028. There is also, separately, a Bluey movie. There’s a good reason for that. As much as rusted-on fans might not like to hear it, key pieces of the Disney ecosystem are showing their age. Star Wars, the home of Luke Skywalker and Princess Leia, turns 50 next year. Marvel’s Cinematic Universe is in phase six, almost two decades after phase one began. Even Thor is starting to look a little long in the hammer.



Another perspective Disney The A-list stars added to Disney’s hall of fame – and what that means for the studio’s future Along with vertical content, however, all roads ultimately lead back to the central content funnel, Disney+. In the past two years the studio has consolidated its assets under the brand, including Hulu, its US-streamer, which is now tucked inside the Australian Disney+ app, and its sports streaming app, ESPN. Eric Schrier, the president of Disney Television Studios, said the strategy was intended to join dots for new audiences, who have not watched older, institutional content such as The Simpsons, Star Wars or even Disney live-action films, but might sample them via the streamer’s vertical and other content. “It gives us an opportunity to take a generation that is consuming most of this content in short form and introducing them to something like The Simpsons,” Schrier told the D23 press briefing. “They may not watch the traditional Simpsons show. They may see clips online, they may see curation, and then eventually become fans of The Simpsons and watch the whole show completely.” And all of this comes as Hollywood obsesses about vertical dramas, the phone-sized, modestly budgeted soap operas which have effectively turned handbags into home entertainment consoles.



Last month, Atlanta hosted the first vertical film festival, Vertex Micro Fest, which focused on short-form vertical content, “micro-dramas” and “AI-powered” stories, while Los Angeles last week hosted Verticon, a fan convention where fans and vertical drama stars pressed the flesh for three days. Verticon also played host to the Verties, the vertical content world’s answer to the Emmys or Oscars. The best actor and actress awards went to Cayman Cardiff (Seducing My Hockey Rival) and Nicole Mattox (Found a Homeless Billionaire Husband for Christmas); vertical of the year was the romantic thriller Swipe Left: Dying for Love, from indie studio muVpix. Discussing Disney’s future: Content creator Blake Silva, Disney executives Eric Schrier and Erin Teague, and moderator (and creator) Jon Youshaei. The Walt Disney Company/Image Group L.A. Setting aside the eyebrow-raising titles, the vertical content business is now worth about $US150 billion globally; vertical dramas account for about $US14 billion of that. At Disney, the vertical strategy was initially tested as a sidebar product within the company’s ESPN ecosystem, before being rolled out widely. What testing in sport revealed, Teague said, was that time-challenged consumers were seeking a way of engaging with the major hits.



Editor's pick Film & TV production The palm-of-your-hand soap operas turning viewers away from TV “There’s no replacement for the live sports viewing experience, but ... thinking about the different ways people are busy, there’s a fight for attention,” Teague said. “People are consuming the live content, but they’re also catching up with key plays, with highlights, and all of that content is short, and actually better natively for a mobile consumption experience,” she said. Teague said viewer engagement had doubled since Verts were launched. In the end, however, replacing legacy IP with enduring appeal will be tough. Disney’s vertical content play can map the Star Wars universe infinitely outward, but few characters can match Princess Leia or Darth Vader for audience recognition, engagement and loyalty. “There will never be a replacement for that long-form original content,” Teague said. “But what is interesting is the way that it is now being supplemented by the shorter form analysis, the clips. Similarly, [in sport] there’s no replacement for the live game. But the additional commentary and analysis around the game is just as interesting.



“The ways that we can merge those experiences to give people exactly what they want, when they want it in a split second, is the challenge.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Clinging to hope: Relatives of missing Sydney family arrive in Nepal
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods Clinging to hope: Relatives of missing Sydney family arrive in Nepal Bishal Karki Zach Hope and August 30, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bidur, Nepal: Relatives of a missing Australian family have arrived in remote Nepal in the desperate hope of finding their loved ones among the survivors rescued from last Wednesday’s deadly floods. The four brothers spoke to this masthead from an army camp at the Nepalese town of Bidur, as helicopters - often carrying injured or shaken survivors - landed roughly every 10 minutes from obliterated regions upstream. Kishore Ramaswamy (left) and Karthik Venkatachalam (right) arrive in a remote part of Nepal to search for their brother Sreedharan Iyer and his family. KATE GERAGHTY Missing is their eldest brother, Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife Lakshmi, 49, and the couple’s two sons, Rudhra, 20, and Rishab, 23. The family, from the Sydney suburb of Cherrybrook, was travelling with a group of about 15 Australian friends to the Hindu sacred site of Mount Kailash when an ice avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border sent water surging downstream, wiping out villages and leaving more than 2000 people dead or missing.



“Not a single person, be it from the embassy, army or rescue team operations have been able to give us a lead concrete enough to say, ‘my family is there’,” Ganesh Gopalakrishnan said on Saturday. “[But] they have been very helpful. And we have positivity.” The two Sydney brothers Rudhra Iyer and Rishab Iyer were travelling with their parents when the disaster struck. Ganesh was at work in Bangalore when he first learned the shocking news that a disaster was unfolding exactly where his family members were travelling. “We didn’t have the itinerary with us so we had to start from scratch, starting with the tour operator,” he said.



“From there we found the itinerary and the place they spent that last night and morning, and then when they would have checked out. That was 8.45am.” Related Article Floods ‘I must look for my sons’: A farmer’s extraordinary survival in Nepal The timeline meant the tour group was leaving the Hotel Kalaish only minutes after the avalanche upstream. “They were on their way towards the border check post [to get to Mount Kalaish],” Ganesh said. “It could have been they were face to face with the floods coming at them, and we just hope they managed to park their cars and escape to an elevated area.” None of the 52 people on the tour, which includes 35 Australians, have been found. Nor has any of the 11 vehicles they were travelling in.



The combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 676 on Saturday, but it is likely to rise sharply because almost 3000 people, including 41 Australians, are still missing. Loading More than 3700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Lakshmi runs the Leap Pad Early Learning Centre in Riverstone, the brothers said. Sreedharan is a mortgage broker. Their eldest son, Rishab, is a doctor, while Rudhra is studying medicine at a university in Sydney. “It is [Sreedharan’s] dream to get his children to become doctors,” Ganesh said. “He’s been very successful in getting two fine boys.”

World.title: How can we invest for our grandkids when markets are so volatile?
World.content:
August 30, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Currently, I have investment bonds for my grandchildren invested in a high-growth option, given the money will sit in their for a long time. With the arrival of a new child, and perceived increased uncertainty in the market, is this still the way forward? Should I now be taking a more conservative approach? In a word, no. There is always market noise, and if we look for it, a reason to convince ourselves to sit on the side lines. Markets today are no more uncertain than they were last year, or 10 years ago. They will rise around 4 out of 5 years. Negative years will happen, and are part of investing. Volatile markets are part and parcel of any long-term investment strategy. Simon Letch The higher returns you receive from stock market investments is the compensation you get for tolerating occasional negative returns. This investment for your new grandchild will likely run 20 years plus. Over that time span the positive years will significantly outweigh the negative. Your current strategy is a good one, stick to it.



My wife and I are in our 70s and have a self-managed super fund in pension mode. We find the fees are becoming prohibitive. We would like to sell our portfolio and join an industry fund. Would you have any advice on how to transition over, as we are not confident in selling our fund? Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Should I sell my $1m investment property and put it into my super? Noel Whittaker Money columnist You are on the right track with regards the process. First, you would each open accounts with your super fund of choice. Next you would liquidate the assets in the SMSF. If it is a share portfolio you could have your cash in three days. Property assets will take longer, and if you have term deposits, you may need to wait for them to mature. Where you want to get to, is having your total SMSF balance held in cash. You would then work in concert with your fund’s accountant to get the monies rolled over from the SMSF to your new accounts via the SuperStream system. It is crucial to get this step right. Do not try and DIY this element.



It needs to be a rollover rather than a withdrawal. Done incorrectly you could have contribution cap and potentially transfer balance cap problems. Typically, you’d leave a few thousand dollars behind in the SMSF to cover wind-up costs. With regard to having the confidence to pull the trigger on this, perhaps you could lean on the fund’s accountant, or the financial planner who assists you with the SMSF. My mother, aged 90, is of sound mind and lives independently on her own and in her own home. She receives a defined benefit pension of $55,000 pa. She needs another $25,000 pa to cover all her living expenses. She recently sold an investment property and netted $1.4 million which is currently invested in term deposits. She is interested in very low-risk investments with a minimum of administration. Are there alternate investment options or structures that would reduce tax liabilities relative to term deposits? Thanks for your question. From what you describe the term deposits seem like a pretty good fit here. Her tax liability would be negligible. She could use insurance bonds, however these pay tax within the bond at 30 per cent, which would almost certainly be higher than the rate of tax your mother would pay. The term deposit interest will be more than she needs for her $25,000 per year income shortfall, so she could reinvest the surplus to help her investment sum maintain its purchasing power.



Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Financial Services. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. Questions to: paul@financialautonomy.com.au Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Victor spent three nights waiting in a Sydney ED. He left without finishing his treatment
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare Victor spent three nights waiting in a Sydney ED. He left without finishing his treatment Rachel Rasker August 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victor Ishak spent three nights waiting in Bankstown’s emergency department with his left leg swelled to almost double its size, and barely able to walk. The 70-year-old was sent to the ED by his GP, who immediately saw the potential red flags. He spent last Friday night on a hard chair in the hospital’s public reception area, as other patients slept on the floor, then the next two nights on a chair that reclined – but not enough to sleep. Victor Ishak spent three nights in Bankstown’s emergency department. George Chan “It was like a halfway house,” Ishak said. “We’re not in a Third World country, we shouldn’t be in systems like this.” By Monday evening – his fourth night in the ED – Ishak was told there were simply not enough beds: “They gave us all an option to either stay where we were in those chairs, or to go home.”



Ishak said although his ankle still resembled “a baby elephant” he chose to sleep in the comfort of his own bed. He returned the next day to see a specialist, with Liverpool Hospital to contact him about taking a sample from his leg. Liverpool did not contact him until Thursday, after this masthead had contacted NSW Health media. Ishak was discharged with no improvement to his swelling. George Chan According to his discharge summary, Ishak was still awaiting the results of 21 tests when he left the hospital. Australian Medical Association NSW president Dr Fred Betros said in an ideal world Ishak would not have been discharged before physicians had received results. “Sometimes it’s an error not to ask for a test, but I think it’s a bigger error to ask for a test and then not know the result before you decide to send someone home.”



In a statement, South Western Sydney LHD apologised to Ishak, and said they were providing follow-up care and support. “During busy periods, some patients may experience longer than expected time in the emergency department while seriously unwell patients are prioritised for emergency care,” the statement read. “We acknowledge it is difficult and frustrating for people when they wait for longer than they expect … and we thank the community for their patience.” Victor Ishak called Bankstown’s ED a “circus”. George Chan Patients across the state are waiting for increasingly prolonged periods, particularly in Sydney’s outer suburbs.



One in 10 patients across NSW waited more than 24 hours to be treated and admitted to a ward or transferred to another hospital in the first quarter of 2026, according to NSW Bureau of Health Information data. That wait time has jumped more than two-and-a-half hours compared to the same period last year. In south-western Sydney, one in 10 patients waited over 28 hours to be admitted, while 10 per cent of Bankstown patients waited about 27 hours. In a bid to address the escalating crisis, the NSW government announced a $130 million investment in a further 22 short-stay recliner chairs at emergency wards across NSW on Monday. These spaces are only intended to house patients for between four and 24 hours. While he acknowledged the privacy of the recliner was more comfortable than the reception area, Ishak spent over 77 hours in Bankstown’s emergency department, and was never offered a bed. Dr Rachael Gill, the NSW branch chair of the Australian College of Emergency Medicine, said it was clear no inpatient beds were available.



“Short stay would not have met this person’s need,” she said, “which is why we’re advocating for an expansion of inpatient capacity [to relieve pressure on emergency]”. Related Article Hospitals The billion-dollar Sydney hospital that’s performing worse than ever Betros agreed, and said while short stay units served a purpose, they were a “Band-Aid solution”. “The long-term solution is having a hospital process that is set up to deal with the patient completely, from the front door all the way to the exit,” he said. “That means getting them into the wards, getting them into their beds, getting their appropriate treatment, and then having the ability to discharge them in a timely manner.”



The NSW government has long blamed clogged hospitals on the Commonwealth, due to the influx of elderly and disabled patients who are medically well enough to be discharged, but who are awaiting a federally funded NDIS or aged care bed. Just 802 new residential aged care places were added in 2024-25, compared to an average of 1800 per year in the previous four financial years. By the federal government’s own projections, Australia needs about 10,600 beds per year to keep up with current demand. NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said there were almost 1100 patients waiting in a NSW hospital for an aged care bed, a figure which has almost doubled over the past year. He said the state government was investing $35.7 million in interim services to help older people transition safely out of hospital while awaiting placement or home supports, which would free up the equivalent of about 180 beds per year. Federal Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said the Albanese government has made record investments in the residential aged care and home care system, including $2 billion in the year’s budget to support 5000 more aged care beds each year. Rae said he would continue working with states and territories to ensure older Australians aren’t stuck in hospital.



Eight days waiting for test results Patients at the heart of the crisis say delays in testing are another part of the story. Michael Hirschhorn presented at Westmead’s emergency department with a suspected foot infection on a Wednesday evening in February, and was given a bed the next day. He said a doctor ordered an MRI of his foot on Thursday at noon, but it was not performed until Monday. “Apparently, they don’t do it over the weekend.” Michael Hirschhorn said he took up a bed unnecessarily at Westmead while awaiting MRI results. Janie Barrett He did not receive his results until the following Thursday, a week after his MRI was initially ordered, eight days since he initially presented to hospital. Hirschhorn’s result was negative, and he was discharged that evening.



“I was blocking a bed … just waiting for someone to read the MRI,” he said, with his only other treatment a daily antibiotic. “That bed could have been occupied by someone in a more serious situation.” A doctor at Westmead ED not authorised to speak publicly expressed frustration at what they called a “dysfunctional” hospital, with 20 or 30 people taking up beds at any one time while waiting for results. The doctor said despite being a major hospital, Westmead’s MRI service only operates on weekdays, with results outsourced to an external company in Melbourne, leaving already strained hospital staff to chase up delayed reports. “The other day I discharged a patient to get an MRI as an outpatient, because that would be quicker than getting an MRI at Westmead,” the doctor said.



Gill said healthcare should be considered a seven day a week necessity. “Because the community doesn’t choose when they’re unwell and when they need to access healthcare.” In a statement, Western Sydney Local Health District said MRIs are prioritised according to clinical urgency, while their CT and X-ray services are available 24/7. The spokesperson said NSW Health is currently assessing opportunities to improve equitable access to imaging services across the state.
