World.title: Springboks bounce back to defeat All Blacks
World.content:
The All Blacks scored four tries to the Springboks' three tries but the hosts kicked several penalty goals to help claim a seven-point victory in front of a sold out crowd of about 60,000.

South Africa came flying out of the blocks and were the first to score with midfielder Jesse Kriel going over near the posts after a strong lineout drive on the right edge of the field.

Wing Cheslin Kolbe kicked the conversion to make it 7-0 to the Springboks in just the third minute of the match.

The All Blacks were having some issues at lineout time but they struck back with a try of their own with a lovely backline move resulting in a break to wing Will Jordan. He fed the ball inside to halfback Cam Roigard who scored under the posts.

Cam Roigard goes in for a try. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

First-five Ruben Love added the extras to tie the game at 7-7 after 16 minutes, though the Springboks kicked a penalty goal soon after to retake the lead 10 points to 7.

The Springboks and the DHL Stadium crowd were fired up and the hosts were next to score a try with midfielder Damian de Allende barging his way over a few phases after another lineout drive in the All Blacks 22.

Kolbe was successful with the conversion to extend South Africa's advantage to 17-7 midway through the first half.

The All Blacks absorbed some more pressure before going on the offensive and captain Ardie Savea made a break down field before the visitors spun the ball wide to fullback Damian McKenzie who scored in the right corner.

Damian McKenzie scores for the All Blacks. BackpagePix/ Samuel Shivambu

Love nailed the tricky conversion to cut South Africa's lead to 17-14 with ten minutes remaining in the first half.

The Springboks were awarded a penalty close to the All Blacks line with just a few minutes left in the first half and chose to take a scrum.

The All Blacks stopped the pushover attempt but South Africa weren't to be denied with captain Siya Kolisi surging over close to line a few phases later.

Kolbe kicked the extra two points to give the Springboks a 24-14 lead going into halftime.

Siya Kolisi celebrates his try with his Springbok teammates. BackpagePix

The Springboks landed the first punch of the second half with Kolbe kicking a penalty goal to extend their advantage to 27-14 in the 49th minute.

The hosts were on a roll and were awarded another penalty close to the All Blacks 22 with the tourists pinged for holding on at a ruck. Kolbe nailed the penalty kick to put the hosts ahead 30-14 with half an hour remaining.

The All Blacks really needed to be next to score to stay in the game and they did just that with wing Leroy Carter outsprinted the cover defence to dive over in the left corner after some nice passing from Fabian Holland and Quinn Tupaea.

Leroy Carter on his way to the tryline. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

Love missed the conversion with the score 30-19 to the Springboks with 13 minutes left.

South Africa hit back not long after with Kolbe kicking a penalty goal from 40 metres out to extend the hosts advantage to 33-19 with about nine minutes remaining in the match.

The All Blacks hit back with a try to Savea and Love nailed the conversion to make it a seven point game at 33-26 with just a few minutes remaining.

That's how the score would remain with the Springboks hanging on to claim the win and level the four match series 1-1.

The third test is in Johannesburg next weekend.

Review all the action in our blog below:

All Blacks squad: 1. George Bower, 2. Codie Taylor, 3. Tyrel Lomax, 4. Fabian Holland, 5. Tupou Vaa'i, 6. Simon Parker, 7. Luke Jacobson, 8. Ardie Savea - Captain, 9. Cam Roigard, 10. Ruben Love, 11. Leroy Carter, 12. Jordie Barrett, 13. Quinn Tupaea, 14. Will Jordan, 15. Damian McKenzie

World.title: Firefighters search for one missing in Henderson housefire
World.content:
One person remains unaccounted for, following a large housefire in Henderson Valley in Auckland.

Thirty-five firefighters were at the scene of the fire.

Fire and Emergency says it received calls about the incident just after 8.30pm Saturday.

Shift manager Garreth Lewis said the house was totally ablaze when crews arrived.

Six trucks, as well as one command unit and one hazardous materials unit, were sent to the scene.

Lewis said crews were searching for the person, along with fighting the fire.

World.title: Thousands of youths to lose access to unemployment benefits after welfare law change
World.content:
Thousands of youths across the country are set to lose access to unemployment benefits, after a welfare bill passed into law under urgency on Friday night.

From November 2026, the government will end Jobseeker payments to 18-19-year-olds whose parents earn more than $67,225.

The limit was originally just over $65,000 when the policy was announced, but has since been adjusted.

In October last year, it was estimated that about 4300 young people would become ineligible for support as a result.

Social Development and Employment Minister Louise Upston said the legislation reflected the government's commitment to reduce benefit dependency and encourage people into work.

"This legislation reinforces the expectation that young people who are not in employment, education or training should be financially supported by their parents, not by taxpayers through the welfare system," she said.

"New Zealanders deserve a welfare system that is firm, fair and simple."

The bill also makes changes to how accommodation supplements are calculated.

Upston said the changes would "better target that support to those who need it most".

"Importantly, it does not apply to homeowners who are receiving New Zealand superannuation, veteran's pension, supported living payment, or the emergency benefit that is the equivalent to the supported living payment.

Shift manager Murray Dunbar said crews pulled one occupant out of the plane.

A Hato Hone St John spokesperson said a patient was transported to Whanganui Base Hospital in a serious condition.

World.title: Heavy rain for upper North Island, avalanche risk ongoing for South Island
World.content:
A flood alert has been issued for Warkworth and forecasters have upgraded weather warnings for the upper North Island, as heavy rain is expected to sweep down from the north through into early Sunday, while strong wind watches and avalanche warnings are in place for parts of the South Island.

On Saturday, MetService upgraded earlier weather watches to orange Heavy Rain Warnings, for Northland, Auckland, Coromandel Peninsula, Bay of Plenty, and some parts of Tai Rāwhiti.

Up to 100mm could fall at rates up to 40mm an hour, though localised downpours could mean even higher amounts. The warnings were expected to be in place until 2am Sunday for Auckland, 3am for Coromandel, and 5am for Bay of Plenty and Tai Rāwhiti.

MetService warned people in all orange heavy rain warning areas to clear their drains and gutters, avoid low-lying areas and drive carefully. Waterways could rise rapidly.

A yellow heavy rain watch was also in place for Waikato.

Flood warning for Warkworth river, Aucklanders warned localised rain could be intense

Auckland Emergency Management (AEM) said a flood alert had been issued for Falls Road in Warkworth, on the Mahurangi River: "Please avoid taking Falls Road, particularly the sections where the road fords the river or that are typically affected by flooding".

People in the Falls Road area of Warkworth should delay travel if they could, it said: "Stay safe - never drive through floodwaters".

The Mahurangi River was already swollen by late Saturday afternoon, Auckland Emergency Management general manager Adam Maggs said, and there had been steady rain throughout the day.

Auckland's Hisbiscus Coast Highway was closed between Hatfields Beach and Waiwera on Saturday night.

AEM said a slip had been reported, and an assessment was being carried out. A spokesperson says there were no signs of property damage, and traffic management was in place.

The forecast heavy rain in localised patches could mean flooding, Maggs said, and AEM teams would be keeping a close eye on the wider north and northwest parts of Auckland.

"It is very hard to determine where that is going to be. (MetService) are not expecting problems to be broad-scale across the whole region, so we have our contractors focusing on the areas that are typically the hot spots, and we have it well covered."

There had only been a few call outs by late Saturday, which was typical of a rainy wintry day, Maggs said.

In Auckland, any blocked stormwater drainage should be reported to Auckland Council on 09 301 0101.

Avalanche risk and strong wind watches for South Island areas, continued storm mop up in Queenstown

In the South Island, yellow strong wind watches were issued for parts of Southland and Otago, along with some road snowfall warnings, while Queenstown continues its clean up efforts after it was hit by wild weather this week, causing flooding, slips and road closures.

Heavy flooding on Thursday, in Queenstown. RNZ / Katie Todd

On Thursday night, 45 people were evacuated from their homes across the Queenstown Lakes District during the storm. And firefighters went to about 16 flooding-related jobs, in Queenstown, Frankton, Arrrowtown, Wānaka and Lake Hāwea.

Queenstown Mayor John Glover said he hopes residents will be able to return to their homes as soon as possible. He did not know how many people were still unable to return, but was expecting assessments would continue throughout the weekend.

The Civil Defence Welfare Hub at the Queenstown Memorial Centre was still open, Glover said.

On Saturday, the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory (which is run by the Mountain Safety Council) warned there was a high avalanche danger in mountainous areas throughout most of the South Island.

Warnings were issued for many areas, including Aoraki Mt Cook, Arthur's Pass, Ohau, Queenstown, Wānaka, and Aspiring, with some noting varied risks for different places within those areas.

The Avalanche Advisory said the risk was especially high for Aoraki Mt Cook. Unsplash / Corey Serravite

Aoraki Mt Cook, and parts of Queenstown were noted in particular.

Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said it had received reports of significant avalanches coming down to the valley floor: "This is not just a warning to alpine skiers and people heading into high alpine regions and backcountry.

"If people are considering going tramping into sub alpine regions you need to be aware of the hazards above you."

People should check the avalanche forecast before heading into alpine backcountry, Daisley said.

In the North Island, Tongariro and Taranaki were also under considerable risk of avalanches as well.

Roads were impacted in Queenstown's CBD after the storm on Thursday. RNZ / Katie Todd

Traffic congestion after road closures and slips

A number of road closures have also impacted the Queenstown region, which caused significant congestion in the town on Friday.

Fernhill and Sunshine Bay Community Association's Simone Bray said restrictions at the one mile roundabout brought commuters to a standstill.

"We live on the top of a really big hill so there's no active transport option for us either so we were sort of just advised if you don't have to go anywhere just stay at home.

"The traffic was built up but it was taking people about an hour and a half basically just to go down the hill to get into Queenstown, which is normally a four minute drive."

Residents in Fernhill, Sunshine Bay, Queenstown central and Frankton Road were also asked to conserve water.

There had been more than 20 slips, many of them substantial on the stretch between Lake Hāwea and Makarora.

Two cars and their occupants were freed after being trapped between slips on State Highway 6 near Wānaka on Friday.

World.title: NZ lessons for worried Australian real estate agents
World.content:
New Zealand real estate salespeople may be able to offer pointers to their Australian counterparts, as they go through possibly their most significant market downturn in recent years.

Australian media have reported on the struggles of some salespeople, who have posted on social media about the downturn.

One, Liam Cromarty, posted a video telling people not to lowball with their offers, because they could end up insulting the owners.

"I had one buyer who offered more than $100,000 less than the bottom end of the range," he said in the Instagram video.

"The buyer thought they've got all the power, the market is terrible and if the owner wants that price, they're going to have wait years for the market to turn around."

He said the property ended up selling to a buyer who offered a higher price.

"Then the buyer that was trying to convince me and that owner the property was sh** and the market was falling and wasn't worth anywhere near what the owners wanted... they turned around and said we'll pay more than where the current offer's at, and by that stage, the owner said, 'I don't care if they offer $10,000 or $20,000 more, I don't trust them'... so don't lowball the owner."

Australian house prices were down 0.7 percent in July and 1.9 percent over the quarter.

The country has been through downturns in house prices before, although not as large as New Zealand's, but this time, the drop could end up being more significant.

Auckland real estate salesperson Diego Traglia said he had operated in a downturn since 2022.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

"To put it into perspective, our auction success rate went from 92 percent in November 2021 to around 8 percent in 2022. We went from double-digit open home attendance to being lucky to have one or two groups through, all within a relatively short period.

"Agents had to get better at what they were doing. Even experienced, high-performing agents like myself had to sharpen their tools and adapt quickly.

"The best way I can explain the change is this - in 2020 and 2021, it was like going for a run downhill with no weight in your backpack and a fresh bottle of water to keep you hydrated. Fast-forward a year or two, and suddenly you were running uphill with a 20kg backpack and a bottle of lukewarm, salty water.

"It was tough. Buyers didn't want to engage and vendors struggled to come to terms with the fact that property values had dropped around 10 percent in a year."

He said the solution was to be more disciplined.

"Daily training, re-engaging with my mentors, scheduling dedicated calling sessions throughout the week, and building better systems and processes to manage the day-to-day work of helping buyers and sellers.

"Ultimately, I actually enjoy operating in markets like this, because my market share tends to increase. Tough markets expose the difference between average agents, and those who have the discipline, systems and skills to perform regardless of conditions.

"As the saying goes, you find out who's been swimming without their togs when the tide goes out."

Brooke Gibson of Found agreed that going back to basics would help.

"Good agents will always list and sell. When we've had such a high, anyone's become an agent and can do well."

World.title: New Zealanders charged after assault at Sydney immigration detention facility
World.content:
Two New Zealanders and a man from Fiji are facing charges in Australia, after an assault at a Sydney immigration detention facility.

Australian Federal Police were called to the Villawood Immigration Detention Centre following the Thursday attack.

They said the 26-year-old Fijian approached another man and began to strike him, as he entered a common area at the facility.

The two New Zealand men, aged 37 and 24, then entered the same room. Police said they also kicked and struck the victim several times, before attempting to restrain him.

Australian Border Force officers made initial inquiries, before referring the matter to police for further investigation.

The trio were arrested at the detention centre early Friday and taken to Cabramatta Police Station.

They appeared at Fairfield Local Court that day, each charged with one count of affray and one of assault causing actual bodily harm.

All three men were remanded in custody and will re-appear at the court in a fortnight.

The victim received medical treatment at the detention centre, before being transported to Auburn Hospital. He was later discharged and taken back to the immigration facility.

Safety concerns at Villawood

Conditions at the detention centre have previously been in the spotlight.

Earlier this month, it was the subject of a scathing review by the watchdog responsible for inspecting federal detention places in Australia, the Commonwealth National Preventive Mechanism.

The report, which followed an inspection in March, found "serious and systemic concerns about the safety, security, maintenance and overall operation of the facility".

It said the facility security situation was ineffectively managed, with both staff and detainees reporting concerns about their safety.

Some detainees even slept outside sleeping areas, which the report said was due to a range of reasons, including intimidation by other people and concerns about safety.

It also found insufficient staffing, and limited interaction between staff and detainees, which it said would mitigate security risks and reduce the likelihood of incidents occurring.

World.title: Labour pledges $21m for Māori-led trades training
World.content:
Labour is pledging to spend $21 million a year on Māori-led trades training if elected into government.

The party says it would establish a contestable, grant-based fund for Māori providers, including marae and iwi trusts, to deliver training.

The announcement was made today at the party's Māori campaign launch at Wainuiomata Marae in Lower Hutt.

Labour's Māori development spokesperson Willie Jackson said he expected up to 3000 Māori would benefit from the plan.

The programme would include a wide variety of trades, he said, from hairdressing to electrical trades and plumbing, and it did not have an age limit.

He said while young people would benefit, it would also be for older people who hadn't had their chance.

Jackson said Labour had run the programme in government, but it had been cut back under the current coalition government.

"We don't understand why you would shut something down that has been incredibly supportive - so we're reintroducing it," he said.

"National has tried to cut its way to growth. Jobs and opportunities have been lost. Labour will grow the economy from the grassroots up, by backing people with the skills and opportunities to get ahead.

"This is about more than getting someone into a job. It's about helping Māori gain new skills, earn more, and build a secure future for themselves and their whānau."

Jackson said the programme was designed and delivered by Māori, for Māori.

"We know what works... so it's not new at all - so it's just about knowing what succeeds in terms of our community.

"It gives people practical skills alongside the mentoring and practical support they need to compete their training, get into work, and stay in work."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the programme had proven to be a success - of those who completed the previous programme, 81 percent went into employment and 76 percent achieved a training outcome.

He said too many Māori were missing out on the security, better pay and opportunities that come with skilled work.

"Backing Māori trades training will complement Labour's plan to extend Apprenticeship Boost and grow the skilled workforce New Zealand needs," Hipkins said.

Carlton will play an elimination final against Geelong after winning a wildcard clash against Melbourne at the MCG.

World.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional return for South Sydney
World.content:
Jai Arrow has made an emotional return for South Sydney, leading the side out and officially playing his 99th match for the club against Gold Coast.

Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year, has received special dispensation from the NRL to play the opening seconds of the Rabbitohs' final two matches for the year.

He was substituted before kick-off for Cameron Murray and left the field at Skilled Park to a standing ovation.

Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett and former stalwart Jason Clark helped Arrow put his boots on before the match.

The Titans wore a commemorative jersey with Arrow's face on the front.

He played 56 matches for the club from 2018 to 2020.

Arrow will lead South Sydney out again next week in their final game of the regular season against the Sydney Roosters.

Arrow was in tears as he left the field. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It will mark his 100th game for the club and the 180th and final match of his career.

Arrow was in the room when elated Souths players were told about the plan during their team review session on Monday morning.

"We all play a tough sport and we all mean so much to so many people, but it's so special to see what players mean to other players when things are going tough," said Rabbitohs fullback Matt Dufty.

"[Jai] brings a smile to everyone's face. Whatever we can do to give back to him, even if it's a little bit, it's just what we need to do. We're all behind him."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

Murray replaced Arrow before kick off. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of his jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs showed their support by marking tries with 'arrow' celebrations during July.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Magpies legend Pendlebury set to join Gold Coast Suns for 2027 season
World.content:
Collingwood legend and AFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury will move to the Gold Coast Suns in 2027.

Pendlebury, who has played 442 games for the Magpies, will move to the Suns as an unrestricted free agent.

The contract is believed to be a multi-year agreement, where the 38-year-old will play a hybrid coaching and on-field role for two seasons, before moving into an assistant coach role for another two years.

Pendlebury was not offered a new contract to continue his career at Collingwood.

"For the past 21 years, it's been an incredible privilege to be a Collingwood footballer. From walking in the doors as a 17-year-old, to seeing the way everyone at the club has welcomed and embraced my family over all these years is something that is truly special," Pendlebury said in a statement.

"I've spent the majority of my life here and so many of my best memories have come through being part of Collingwood. The friendships, the challenges, the successes and even the tough times have all shaped who I am.

"The privilege of pulling on the Collingwood jumper has never been lost on me. I understand what this club means to so many people and I've always tried to represent it in a way that makes our Magpie Army proud.

"This decision has not come lightly but I know this is the best thing for me and my family as I transition into the next phase of my football journey."

The midfielder will leave the Magpies as one of the club's greatest-ever players, having won two premierships, a Norm Smith medal and six All-Australian nods.

His role at the Suns is set to mimic former Hawthorn legend Luke Hodge's 2018 move to the Brisbane Lions, where Hodge played two seasons as an on-field coach for a young Lions squad that has gone on to win two premierships from three grand final appearances.

The deal will be officially ticked off when the AFL's free agency period begins on October 2.

Pendlebury was denied a finals farewell game in Collingwood's wildcard loss to the Western Bulldogs on Friday night after straining his hamstring in the final game of the regular season.

World.title: Australian talent is the biggest loser in Super Netball signings
World.content:
As the 2027 signing window comes to a close, it's clear great Australian talent will be missing from the Super Netball court next year.

Young shooter Lucy Austin is a dual premiership player and a Diamond. After making her international debut 10 months ago, she was not offered a contract.

24-year-old Lucy Austin moved to the Giants this year and played just four games before a foot injury ruled her out for the rest of the season. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Eight years toiling away on the fringe of selection finally paid off for Sharni Lambden in 2025. However, the lethal midcourter lasted just two seasons before being turfed out of the league.

Then there's the forced retirements of Em Mannix, Maddy Proud and Maddy Turner. Stalwarts of the game that have been squeezed out without a proper goodbye from fans. The former two are mothers that had only just returned from pregnancy and had more to give.

Netballer explains absence after being separated from daughter at birth Emily Mannix talks about her extended absence from the Super Netball league, and why she's now ready to return for the Melbourne Vixens after a "freak accident" meant her daughter Mabel needed emergency care at birth.

There have been some brutal calls made across the eight teams in pursuit of success. Yet nothing has quite rocked the fan base like the loss of Kate Eddy.

The beloved defender won multiple titles during her nine seasons of Super Netball and played a key role in getting the Melbourne Vixens to the past three consecutive grand finals.

Swinging across the wing defence and goal defence positions, Eddy is versatile and a workhorse. She's a team player, great for building culture off the court and the kind of glue that pieces a bunch of superstars together on court.

On Monday, a devastated Eddy revealed a "breakdown in communication" meant she'd not only missed out on the opportunity to recommit to the Vixens but on a Super Netball contract altogether.

Only Jo Weston will remain from the club's premiership-winning defence of 2025. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Although she has secured a non-playing role with the club and could still be picked up as an injury or pregnancy replacement, this has been the final nail in the coffin for Vixens supporters after a series of confusing contracting decisions.

Following a milestone year where the club set a 10,000-membership record, accounting for more than 25 per cent of the league's total membership base, many are now seriously considering whether to renew.

What happened?

There are two very different version of events.

Loading Instagram content

On Monday night, the club issued a member's email responding to backlash, clarifying their preference had been to keep Eddy and that they had offered her a contract, yet were unable to lock in a deal with her management in the timeframe required to finalise their playing list.

They thought Eddy was still assessing her options from rivals and said when the deadlines and subsequent extensions they had given were not met, and the pay increase requested would not fit within their salary cap, they "had no choice but to switch our attention to other players".

According to this side of the story, more than one offer was discussed with Eddy's agent. The club would not confirm whether it tried to contact Eddy directly during this time.

Agent Anthony Panozzo said he was acting on the basis that the negotiations were happening in good faith with five to six days still left for clubs to re-sign existing players and was not told the offer was first and final.

In his discussions, he said he was transparent that Eddy had zeroed in on the Vixens and the deadlines given were loosely timed or unreasonable. For instance, an email seen by ABC Sport sent on Tuesday, August 11 at 6:36pm asked for Eddy's acceptance or rejection "by tonight" without listing a definite time.

There was a challenging time difference as this took place while Eddy was on holiday in Hawaii. After speaking with his client, Panozzo said he countered the Vixens original offer the next morning — Wednesday August 12 at 9:23am — with a pay rise of 7.5 per cent.

Three hours later, the Vixens replied and took the contract off the table. Following that, staff could not be reached by phone despite Panozzo's various attempts.

On this side of the story, only one offer was received by the agent.

Only Kiera Austin from this player huddle will be returning for the Vixens. (Getty: Daniel Pockett)

Although both insist there was no "breakdown in communication", it feels like an accurate assessment from Eddy regarding deadlines and expectations. Ultimately the athlete has got stuck in the crossfire and even if she managed to get to the bottom of it, the truth wouldn't bring the same peace of mind as a full-time playing contract.

The main question is how desperate were the Vixens to keep Eddy? Six players leaving indicates their team is looking to go in a different direction — they will basically have a brand new, younger and taller backline — and there was still plenty of time to re-sign an existing player when they swung the axe.

Official signings for non-existing players didn't open until August 17. There were also reports that Rudi Ellis too was offered a two-year deal before it was revoked, and that both she and Mannix had to call coach Di Honey to find out what was happening with their futures. Ellis has since moved to the NSW Swifts and Mannix has retired.

Thunderbirds win record-breaking Super Netball title The Adelaide Thunderbirds have unlocked a Super Netball dynasty with a unique coaching approach. The three-time Super Netball champions defeated the Melbourne Vixens 61- 40 in the grand final.

Previously, the club adhered to a quota of 70 per cent Victorian signings. For the past couple of years, they've been the only team made up of 100 per cent Australian talent. Having announced their final roster of 10 on Thursday, the number of Victorians has dropped from eight to three, while three New Zealand Silver Ferns imports will join the team.

The clean-out has been hard for fans to comprehend. Although the Vixens lost the grand final by a record margin, they still finished in the top two and won a title as recently as 2025.

"We need to ensure the Vixens remain competitive in a Super Netball competition where the standards keep getting higher each season," a statement provided to ABC Sport read.

"After finishing runners-up, we determined to look further afield to enhance key areas of our line-up, particularly to add height and versatility across the court.

"That view coincided with considerable interstate player movement, as well as rule changes in New Zealand that have opened access to world-class talent from across the Tasman.

"This will result in fewer Victorians in our squad this year, however, we remain fully committed to our Victorian pathways and nurturing and prioritising local talent."

Why has this happened?

The delay in finalising Super Netball's collective player agreement (CPA) didn't help. It pushed back the signing window to coincide with the end of the UK Superleague window and meant there were less contracts available in England to offer by the time Australian players were finding out they weren't going to be asked back.

Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026 Messy and drawn-out pay negotiations are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the Aussie Diamonds.

The situation across the ditch is extremely dire. Due to the poor mismanagement by Netball New Zealand, it's likely their elite competition won't exist next year. This, as well as a change in Silver Ferns eligibility rules has led to an influx of Kiwi stars.

With an unlimited import rule, the international playing cohort in Super Netball rises from 20 to 24 (with Sydney Sirens still yet to announce half their team). It might not sound that much higher, but with only 80 full-time contracts on offer and an increase from eight to 12 Silver Ferns in the competition, it means you could sign an entire Kiwi team and still have a couple left over.

Plus, Netball Australia cancelled its plans to add more teams and expand, which would've opened up more opportunity for homegrown talent.

What happens now?

The club wellbeing leads will no longer hold the responsibility or have the capacity to check in on departing players, so the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA) will help them transition out of the game.

Only two players from the New Zealand Silver Ferns gold-medal winning team in Glasgow are yet to be signed to Super Netball teams. (Getty: Mattia Ozbot)

An exit meeting is held to offer support and run through the list of services they can access. Former Australian captain Nat von Bertouch as the ANPA Alumni and Diamonds wellbeing manager checks in frequently for the first two years before they join the past player pool that can contact her anytime. This group features athletes from way back to the Commonwealth Bank Trophy era of the 1990s and enables them to still feel connected to the sport.

Former Australian skipper Natalie von Bertouch during the 2012 Quad Series. (Getty: Tony Feder)

Players automatically get a certificate of foundation coaching level and ANPA ensures they leave the clubs properly. Financial and legal advice can also be provided.

"Some people are keen to engage straight away, some are really hurt and lost and not sure where to start, so we are there to meet the athlete whenever they're ready," Von Bertouch said.

"Whether they've left on their own terms or not, people often are seeking connection and as a sport we haven't done that amazingly well, so it's nice that they can join a wider group of women that want to support one another."

World.title: AFL in bind over future concussion insurance for players
World.content:
The report into Geelong player Jake Kolodjashnij's concussion waiver was conspicuous because of an absence.

The AFL's independent investigator into the matter, James Peters KC, did not find that Geelong erred by allowing Kolodjashnij to sign an "acknowledgement of risk" letter absolving Geelong from its legal obligations.

In order to continue his career after the AFL's Concussion Panel couldn't give a firm yes or no on whether he could keep playing, Kolodjashnij agreed to take on the legal risk of damage or injury that might arise from any future concussions.

The AFL fined Geelong $140,000 ($40,000 was for a suspended sanction from a separate incident last year) for altering Kolodjashnij's contract outside the standard playing contract and for failing to lodge that document with the AFL.

Jake Kolodjashnij of the Cats is yet to return to the AFL after concerns were raised about a waiver he signed. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

But not because there was anything intrinsically wrong with what was in that letter.

"We do not make any adverse findings against Geelong or its Board for deciding to enter into an agreement with Mr Kolodjashnij seeking to mitigate the legal exposure to Geelong," Peters wrote in his summary.

That statement is significant because it doesn't rule out the possibility of another player entering into a similar agreement down the track.

That's clearly important because we know football players will do almost anything to keep playing.

Moreover, with an average AFL salary of about $500,000 per year, ending a career prematurely can have massive financial implications for players.

So, can it happen again?

Both the league and the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) are adamant that it can't.

Andrew Dillon says the AFL and players' association would not approve any similar waivers. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Grilled on Thursday, AFL CEO Andrew Dillon said any similar waiver brought to the attention of the league and the Players Association would not be approved.

"If that [a proposed waiver] takes away from the minimum terms that have been bargained for by the Players Association … it would require approval from the Players Association," Dillon said.

"So, that wouldn't occur if the PA wasn't across that — and they weren't in this case and that's why the waiver has been moved by Geelong," he said.

Kolodjashnij hasn't returned to the playing field since the story about his waiver blew up.

The CEO of the AFL Players Association, James Gallagher, said he was the subject of ongoing medical assessment.

When questioned on radio station SEN, Gallagher was even more adamant that no future concussion waivers would see the light of day.

"Anything that looks like it could possibly change the terms and conditions of a player's employment has to come to both the AFL and the AFLPA for approval," Gallagher said

"And quite clearly if it relates to a player's health and safety, those things won't be approved moving forward.

"So that's abundantly clear out of this now; a silver lining maybe from a really difficult situation that everyone's been navigating," Gallagher said.

But as Gallagher suggested, this really difficult situation is a minefield for the AFL and its players.

Angus Brayshaw was forced to retire because of repeated concussions. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

The problem is insurance.

Zurich Insurance, which provides cover for the AFLPA's superannuation fund, decided earlier this year that it would no longer pay total and permanent disability benefits for players who suffered traumatic head injury, concussion, CTE, post-concussion syndrome or any neurological impairment linked to brain injury.

Previously Zurich was paying out up to $1.1 million.

The AFLPA subsequently wrote to other insurers, asking them to fill the breach, but none came forward.

As it is, players are now only covered through the PA, which has a $54 million Injury and Support Fund that covers the length of the current collective bargaining agreement (CBA).

That fund is paid for by the players.

Players can be paid up to $500,000 under the Football Ending Injury Benefit program, which covers mental health services, dental and more severe injuries like concussion.

There's also a severe injury benefit worth up to $600,000 for players whose impacts are so great that they can have an impact on their future work.

The AFL and the PA have agreed to conduct a review given the dearth of insurance options and the enormity of the concussion issue.

The game finds itself in a precarious situation: The risks of severe concussion and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) are now widely known and understood.

The AFL and the players' association have announced a review of concussion issues in the game. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

The underlying question about how to run a contact sport given those known risks is being answered on the run, not only by the AFL but by all collision sports around the world.

If sporting codes are going to allow players to put their body and brains on the line, they also have to provide protection for those players if they're injured.

"The challenge that's facing the industry as a whole is how risk is looked at, how the insurance is looked at, and how the safety net for players and officials is looked at," Dillon said this week.

Gallagher said the AFL was going to come to the party to cover the gap left by insurers.

"What's becoming more and more clear is that the game's going to have to do more to provide that safety net rather than looking externally for it," Gallagher said.

"I think that's evident, and part of the agreement between us and the AFL about the work that comes next was, you know, an expansion of the Injury and Support Fund to broaden that safety net," he said.

As it is, the players who are playing in the Wildcard Round this weekend and the finals over September won't have insurance cover outside of the AFLPA if they sustain a traumatic brain injury.

Collingwood star Nick Daicos is featuring during the Wildcard round. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

There's clearly no quick fix.

The best-case scenario is an agreement between the AFL and the PA by the beginning of next season.

However, with the current CBA between the players and the AFL running out at the end of next season, any new agreement on concussion payments could be put off until then.

The joint review will also cover broader issues around concussion, including clearer protocols for the AFL Concussion Panel.

Problems arose when the panel reviewed Kolodjashnij and gave an "amber" finding regarding his risk to continue playing.

"There needs to be clarity whether a player is fit to play or not," Gallagher said.

There are also plans to limit contact training at AFL and AFLW clubs.

The Players Association's attitude is that concussion is the most significant issue in the game by a country mile.

A class action next year led by former Geelong player Max Rooke will hear arguments that he was left with brain damage because of the actions of the AFL and his club.

The court's decision could change the AFL landscape.

Players' health and safety is obviously the top concern, but the broader issue of how they can function after their brief football careers are over if they suffer a traumatic brain injury remains a work in progress.

World.title: Paralympic champ out to conquer 'hardest' course at Sydney Marathon
World.content:
Madison de Rozario is beaming, posing for photos and conducting interviews, in the shadows of the Sydney Harbour Bridge as she prepares for a massive moment in her career.

Originally from Perth, she is now a long-time Sydneysider, sharpening her skills as one of Australia's greatest wheelchair racers on the roads around Olympic Park under the guidance of legendary coach Louise Sauvage.

But this weekend she is hoping to tame the 42-kilometre route from North Sydney to the Opera House and win her third Sydney Marathon, but first with its status as a World Major, granted last year.

"It's quite bizarre doing a marathon through parts of Sydney that you've hung out in very different contexts," she told ABC Sport.

"Like going down Oxford Street, I'm like, I've been here, but not doing this. So it's quite a cool experience to do.

"And then on the other hand, it's such a tricky course that I dread it. Of all the majors, it's the hilliest. I find it the most difficult.

"I'm dying to race at home in Australia and Sydney, and then also I'm like 'oh, but does it have to be just the hardest 42 kilometres that we have?'"

Loading Instagram content

Marathon mindset

While the picturesque course tests the toughest competitors, it is one de Rozario has conquered twice before, including most recently in 2024, days after returning from the Paris Paralympics.

"That was one of the most emotional roller coaster two weeks of my life," she said.

De Rozario carried the Australian flag at the opening ceremony at the Paris Games before learning her father had died.

She then competed in the marathon and 5,000m, winning silver and bronze respectively.

"I think it was just the way to round out the Paris Paralympics, and then Sydney Marathon is one of the most incredible … most emotional races I've ever done in my life," she said.

"And so I think that'll always be so special to me, to come into the Opera House [at the finish line] and have that moment."

The two-time Paralympic gold medallist en route to victory in the 2024 Sydney Marathon. (AAP: Steve Markham)

The 32-year-old made a late decision not to race the event last year, as it earned coveted Major status.

"To drop a race at home and to watch something that you feel like you've been a part of in creating was a hard watch," she said.

"But I think there's something really cool about seeing international women wheelchair racers racing in Australia at an event in a city that I live in, in a sport that I love so much."

De Rozario has won three marathon majors, and marathon and 800m Paralympic gold medals at the Tokyo Paralympics.

After launching her international career on the track as a 14-year-old at the Beijing 2008 Paralympics, she is now going all in on the longest distance.

The Perth product claimed silver in the marathon at the Paris 2024 Paralympics. (Getty Images: Marco Mantovani)

"I haven't been on a track since Paris and to just focus on the marathon has been really amazing," she said.

"And I think that makes these really technical marathons like Sydney so much more exciting because there isn't that [thought in the] back of your head 'we have to back up for the speed of the track', and bring something else into it.

"This is it for the year. I have two more races, two really hilly marathons, and that gets to be our entire focus, and that's been really nice."

Legendary McFadden to take on Sydney

De Rozario is the local headline act this year, but arguably the best female wheelchair marathoner in history will line up alongside her.

The US's Tatyana McFadden, 37, is a nine-time Paralympic champion, and has 24 World Marathon Major wins, the most of any woman.

Tatyana McFadden is a legend of wheelchair track and road racing. (Getty Images: Alex Davidson)

"It was just on my list to do it and to go back and to really try to tackle this course," she said.

"I heard it was really challenging, and I like challenging things."

McFadden has competed in six Summer Paralympics and one Winter Games, and has dominated on the track and the road across an impressive career.

"I think it's just constantly growing and constantly learning. I feel like if you're not learning or growing you just can't get to that next level," she said.

McFadden was diagnosed with a severe blood clotting disorder in 2017, which threatened to end her career.

It was a 20-month road to recovery, but it made her more appreciative of maintaining such a high level of performance over decades.

"I know in my heart this is the path I still want to go on, and I know that I can do it. And I just need to find those people to come along with me," she said.

"So I've been really lucky and blessed with that. And it's been such a great year this year already, with third in Boston, second in London, and two world records on the track."

McFadden was also eyeing off a home Paralympics in LA in 2028, and it was one she hoped could capture the public's attention.

Tatyana McFadden is the USA's most decorated female track and field Paralympian. (Getty Images / Tokyo 2020: Atsushi Tomura)

"My challenge for the US is really to put Paralympics first, because everyone knows the Olympics, right?" she said.

"But for the Paralympic side, I think we need that continuous growth and effort because when you look at the mainstream media, we're still not mentioned.

"So it's really important that we continue that pressure."

She said a lot could be learned from the Marathon Majors like Boston, Chicago, and New York in their approach to elevating Para athletes.

"There's many different sports, and we need to start covering all those sports and showing how athletes can play soccer and bocce and the swimming and the archery and the table tennis. There's so many different summer sports out there besides the wheelchair racing that we need to showcase," she said.

"And I think also supporting our local para sports programs.

"We're a big country, and there's a lot of para sports programs. And so I think [we need to] continue to advocate for those."

Tech.title: Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony Music and Warner Chappell have filed suit against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking damages for “tens of thousands” copyrighted works. The companies are asking for up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance when identifiable copyright data was stripped. In total, the damages could amount to several billion dollars if a court finds in Sony and Warner’s favor and awards the maximum amount.

In addition to suing Anthropic as an entity, the complaint names Co-Founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann as individual defendants. The suit alleges that Mann used BitTorrent to download over five million pirated books, and that employees downloaded at least two million more from Pirate Library Mirror. It also claims that Anthropic scraped lyrics from sites like MusixMatch and LyricFind, which paid to license content from the labels.

According to the filing:

Plaintiff Music Publishers, a group of the world’s leading music publishers, bring this action to hold accountable the culprits behind one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history. Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic’s “Claude” series of artificial intelligence (“AI”) models.

Specific songs named as being found in Anthropic’s training data include Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell’s “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Bon Jovi’s “Livin’ On a Prayer,” Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September,” Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” and TaylorSwift’s “Paper Rings.” Antrhopic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Distraction-free writing gadget BYOK is adding custom extensions
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

BYOK is a no-frills, single-purpose gadget that 90 percent of people will find absolutely frivolous. But for those who spend a significant chunk of their lives putting words to virtual paper, there is an obvious allure. Personally, I think it’s at its best when you just stick to the bare minimum, focusing on pure text drafting. Certain users, though, need more. They want BYOK to take notes, they want to use it for writing screenplays, or maybe they want to organize a sprawling novel.

Balancing the wants and needs of these more demanding users has been a challenge that BYOK founder Nick Sjolinder has been trying to figure out how to tackle. The answer he seems to have landed on, is scripts. Rather than clutter BYOK with a ton of features that 80 percent of its users wont touch, or crowd the Studio app with even more formats, the company is planning to implement optional scripts that expand the capabilities of BYOK.

A few examples of the kinds of thing people will be able to create are a screenplay assistant, a character note tool, and a writing analyzer. This could let users highlight text in a document and pull it out as a note or tell them when they’re using the passive voice. It’s still early in development and the scripting features haven’t rolled out publicly, but BYOK is asking for feedback from its users.

Tech.title: Welcome to Night Vale cocreator Joseph Fink learned storytelling from Grim Fandango
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Joseph Fink is the cocreator and cowriter of Welcome to Night Vale, arguably the most important fiction podcast ever. He’s also the creator of the noir podcast Unlicensed and Alice Isn’t Dead, which takes some of the conspiratorial cosmic horror of Night Vale and turns it into fodder for a more serious series about relationships, trauma, and the open road. There’s also a sequel series out now called Don’t Tell Alice that takes the story down an even darker path in which protagonist Keisha is the one with a secret.

Joseph is also an accomplished author. In addition to co-writing the three Welcome to Night Vale novels, he’s also penned the Alice Isn’t Dead novel and The Halloween Moon. His latest work is The Nudge, which features some gorgeous illustrations from Jessica Hayworth, who also provides the art for Night Vale, hits shelves on September 1st. It’s a brief and unsettling novella about a man trying to outrun some mysterious evil.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

Podcast Addict. It’s an Android-only podcast app made by one guy named Xavier, and it is so much better than any other podcast app that it’s the main reason I can never switch to an iPhone. I’m maybe the one guy in the entire country who chooses phones based on how they play podcasts.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I use Bluesky, which I used to like because no one was there and so no one read my posts, which is really the ideal social media for me. Now there are more people there, and sometimes people read and respond to my posts, which is a drag.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

My entire understanding of storytelling is probably shaped by Grim Fandango, a 1999 adventure game about a sad sack grim reaper navigating a film noir afterlife. There are lines and images from that game that will live in my head forever, even if a lot of them were parodies or references to classic films I wasn’t even aware existed when I first played that game.

What creation are you most proud of?

Our Audible show Unlicensed was one of those few projects that turned out exactly how I wanted it to in my head. A mystery series set in the least cool parts of Los Angeles, the parts where the actual people live. I didn’t want it to be “good for two writers who usually don’t write mysteries.” I just wanted us to write a damn good mystery, and I think we did. We got three seasons out of Audible, but then they mostly shut down their original shows department, and that was it. If I had my choice though, I’d happily spend the rest of my life writing Unlicensed.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

I recently watched a talk with Meshell Ndegeocello, and she described having to shush a fellow student in a guitar workshop who was noodling on his guitar while the teacher was trying to demonstrate something. Meshell said: “As a musician, it doesn’t matter how well you play if you can’t listen.” I don’t know if it’s the best advice I’ve ever received, but I think it’s damn good advice and applies to a lot of things outside of music.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

I buy too many books, constantly. I like to hang out in bookstores, and I’ve never left one without buying at least a couple of books. I’m mostly not a physical media guy, I have no interest in owning records or DVDs, but I’ll build an addition to my house before I get rid of any books.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

“It turns out watching a guy write audio fiction on his computer is boring, this movie was a mistake sorry, we’re sorry.”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

I don’t really use GIFs or memes. I’m very much a text guy, which is why I stick to text social media mostly, even though that doesn’t really help you sell books or stuff like that.

Tech.title: The Galaxy Z Flip 8 is at its best when there’s friction
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

What do you want from a flip phone when it’s closed? A simple interface, perhaps notifications and a widget or two, for handling the basics? Or a fully fledged Android experience shrunk down for the Flip form factor? For years, Samsung has insisted on the former, even as some fans — and Razr rival Motorola — have pushed for the latter. With the Galaxy Z Flip 8, Samsung has given in.

Although the Z Flip 8’s hardware is almost unchanged year-on-year, Samsung has fundamentally rethought how this phone is meant to be used when shut. The cover screen feels more like a regular Android phone, with easier access to the full versions of every single app, letting you browse social media, watch movies, and play games without ever opening the phone. Not every app works well on a tiny square screen with two cameras in the middle of it, but even when they don’t, that friction between me and the distractions of my phone still feels as much a feature as a bug.

Everything exciting about the Z Flip 8 lies in its 4-inch cover screen, which is now more versatile than ever thanks to a homescreen redesign. Swiping down from the top left now brings up your notifications, while swiping from the top right instead shows a cover-screen-optimized version of the Quick Settings panel. Immediately, this feels more like a phone.

More exciting is what happens when you swipe up from the bottom: you get an app drawer. By default, this is populated with a selection of Samsung’s own apps that are optimized for the square screen, plus a “Labs” section with third-party options including Netflix and WhatsApp. But right below that, Samsung has included an easy prompt to install MultiStar, the Good Lock module that lets you run any app you’d like on the outer screen.

Samsung used to bury the option deep in the phone’s settings, only to be found by those who knew to look for it. The bottom of the app drawer isn’t quite front and center, but it’s much more prominent than it used to be.

You can run any app you’d like on the cover screen. The Withings app scales badly: The graph takes up too much space to even show both axes, and it becomes impossible to scroll past it. Google Maps works, but it’s busy and awkward, especially when you try to zoom in. HBO Max works flawlessly, but it wouldn’t be my first choice to watch Lanterns.

You can still run apps in three forms: full-screen, with the cameras blocking part of the software; a square display that stops just above the level of the cameras; or a thin portrait-aspect ratio that letterboxes the sides. A small virtual button at the bottom of the screen lets you cycle through them.

Good performance isn’t guaranteed. Some apps, like Withings’ health tracker companion app, are almost impossible to use on the cover screen, with no configuration that leaves enough space for its graphs to fit. Google Maps is only a bit better — I love the idea of quickly checking my walking route without opening the phone, but there are so many floating interface elements that it’s unwieldy at best. Others work smoothly, but feel pointless: I can stream HBO Max on the tiny outer display, but I’d never want to.

But for other apps, the new cover screen options feel genuinely freeing. I can open Todoist and tick off a task, dip into WhatsApp to send a message, or open MyFitnessPal to log the snack I just ate. They’re quick actions that work well enough on the small screen, and because other apps — *cough* Instagram *cough* — don’t, I can dive into them without the risk of getting dragged into doomscrolling. That little bit of friction is just enough to save me from wasting 20 minutes I’ll never get back.

Like last year’s phone, the cover screen wraps around the cameras.

As for the hardware, little has changed. The Z Flip 8 is 0.6mm thinner and 8g lighter than its predecessor. This is the thickest of Samsung’s three current foldables, but it’s more compact than Motorola’s Razrs, its only real rivals.

Samsung didn’t upgrade the Z Flip 8 with the thinner, tougher titanium display stack found in the two new Z Fold 8 phones, which also means this has just as visible a crease as ever. It rarely bothers me, and is hard to see head-on, but you may feel differently. The IP48 rating is a more objective issue, and means that while this phone is mostly safe from water, it’s still vulnerable to dust.

On the inside, you’ll find the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 if you’re in the US, though my UK model runs Samsung’s Exynos 2600. Exynos chips get a bad rep, but performance has been smooth so far, and I have no real complaints.

This is the online-exclusive mint, but the phone’s also available in pink, cream, and gray. It’s a little thinner and lighter than before, but not by much. And the crease is still pretty noticeable compared to the two new Fold 8 phones.

As with the Z Fold 8 phones, Samsung switched to more energy-dense silicon-carbon batteries for the Z Flip 8. Unlike those phones, it didn’t actually increase the battery capacity, but instead used smaller cells with the same 4,300mAh capacity — the key to shrinking the phone itself. Still, battery life is solid, reliably lasting the full day with battery to spare. The charging — 25W wired, 15W wireless — is relatively unimpressive, and the only way to get Qi2 charging is still by using a compatible magnetic case.

Storage and RAM remain the same as on the Z Flip 7; the screens do too apart from small bumps to peak brightness, and the cameras are also identical to last year’s. The 50-megapixel main camera is impressive, and especially helpful since the form factor means you can use it for selfies too. The 12-megapixel ultrawide and 10-megapixel inner camera aren’t remarkable, but they get the job done. A slab phone at this price would have better cameras, and most likely a telephoto lens, but the lenses here are good enough.

Previous Next























1 / 13 The main camera mostly gets good results.

The question is whether it’s all good enough for the price, given Samsung has bumped the Z Flip 8 up to $1,199.99, a $100 increase. Z Flip 7 owners certainly shouldn’t upgrade, and anyone else should consider buying that phone instead, since the difference between the two is slight.

After all, the big upgrades are software, and unlikely to remain exclusive. Last year’s Z Flip 7 hasn’t yet been updated to One UI 9, but since its outer screen is almost identical, it seems likely to get the upgraded software, giving one less reason to opt for the new model. The Z Flip 6 and earlier, with their smaller cover screens, seem more likely to miss out. I’ve asked Samsung about its upgrade plans, but haven’t yet heard back.

Customizable Now Brief cards were added in One UI 9. The camcorder-inspired video recording is still one of the phone’s best features. If you find the full apps frustrating, various cover screen widgets are still available.

Most of the other software upgrades aren’t even Flip-specific. Customizable, AI-powered cards have been added to the daily Now Brief; My FanCam lets you crop video to focus on a specific subject; and Audio Eraser can now dim background noise and highlight dialogue in apps like YouTube and Netflix. You’ll find those features across all of Samsung’s new foldables, plus the new Galaxy S26 FE.

Modest as the Z Flip 8’s hardware upgrades are, it feels like a turning point for Samsung, which is mostly done trying to limit the ways people use the cover screen. Given the speculation that the short, wide Z Fold 8 could replace the Flip form factor as Samsung’s “small phone that unfolds to a big phone,” it makes sense to close the gap between them.

The Z Fold 8 is definitely bigger than the Z Flip 8. But the Flip’s small, obstructed screen is less functional — for better or worse. Open, the Z Fold 8 feels like a compact tablet. While the Flip opens up to a pretty regular phone.

The Z Fold 8 is a more capable phone than the Z Flip 8 when closed, its squat screen more usable than the Flip’s tiny one, despite Samsung’s software upgrades. But I have a real soft spot for the Flip form factor, which is tiny and pocketable when closed and a normal, almost compromise-free flagship phone when open — and endlessly satisfying to flip shut.

More than that, I enjoy its frictions. I welcome Samsung’s move to make it easier to use full apps on the cover screen, but I also welcome that it will never be entirely successful. Some apps simply don’t work on a screen this size, and the Z Flip 8 is all the better for it.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Flip 8, you must agree to: Google Terms of Service

Google Play Terms of Service

Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS

Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.”

Samsung End User Licence Agreement

Samsung Privacy Notice

Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services

“Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”

Send usage and diagnostic data to Google

Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant

Turn on Samsung offline finding

Samsung news and special offers

Samsung personalized advertising

Bixby personal data intelligence

Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements.

Tech.title: Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

For musicians — especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music — the increasingly complicated question of what is “real” and what isn’t feels particularly urgent and personal. Professional courtesy can make this only more complex; listeners can call out performers they suspect of using gen AI, but it’s something else for artists to raise concerns about their professional peers. There are some though, like 26-year-old EDM producer Max “H4RRIS” Harris, who are taking a stand against generative technology with videos calling out anyone they believe is trying to pass off AI slop as human-made art.

When I recently spoke with Harris, he told me that he sees AI-generated music as “a kind of decoy art form,” and he thinks that the people making it don’t really have anything meaningful to say with their creations. He feels that true art in any medium is “created by people that are trying to express feelings and messages,” and he believes that the only thing AI boosters are really interested in is making a quick profit.

“I don’t consider AI-generated material to be art, and I don’t think this technology is really advancing art in any meaningful way,” Harris said. “It’s a technological advancement that’s giving people a way to steal real art and pass it off as their own.”

Harris, originally from Maine, described his approach to making music as being fairly similar to working in other creative mediums. He always begins with a core concept before he starts “throwing more ideas down until I find something that sticks.” And as complicated as his workflow might look to someone unfamiliar with all of the tools and programs that he uses — his production setup includes Ableton Live, Novation Launchkey 49 MIDI controller, Ableton Push 3, Launchpad X, a couple of analog synthesizers, Serum, Diva, and the software sampler Kontakt — he said that the entire process is “really just me making creative decisions” that culminates in a sound that feels right.

“Each of those decisions — and there’s hundreds of them to go into each song — brings me closer to evoking a specific kind of idea or emotion,” Harris explained. “And then once I have a song mapped out, I have to start making even more choices about how to mix it in a way that makes it sound good and presentable.”

In Harris’ view, being a real artist means being able to make those kinds of experimental but informed creative decisions using your own studied understanding of a given medium. One of Harris’ biggest issues with gen AI is the way the technology often eliminates a user’s need to think about how songs (or books, films, podcasts, etc.) come together. But he has also been dismayed at the way that AI posers are muddying listeners’ understanding of what human-made EDM actually sounds like.

“Aside from the similar vocals, you can usually hear a sharp hissing throughout the track,” Harris said of AI-generated songs. “I think that comes from the way that these models often work by starting with a big white noise block and then making guesses about waveforms by referencing data taken from real songs.”

Harris pointed to MANSA’s “Midnight on My Mind” and Danny and Ian Asher’s “Take Me (To The Moon)” as what he thinks are examples of AI-produced songs that embody what he jokingly refers to as “the AI revolution” that’s responsible for polluting the EDM space. MANSA, Danny, and Asher have not publicly commented on whether they use generative tools in their music. But Harris and other EDM fans have noticed the similarities between “Take Me (To The Moon)” and another person’s AI-generated track. There’s no definitive evidence that MANSA produced “Midnight on My Mind” with AI. Harris could very well be wrong about these songs being generated with AI. But his insistence that they are reflects the larger culture of mistrust that has developed in response to the growing presence of AI content online.

“People are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking [AI] to remix them.”

Harris holds AI production company Suno responsible for the recent spike in this kind of music being uploaded to the internet, but he also credits specific quirks of the platform for helping him learn how to spot songs worth calling out.

“Something I’ve noticed with a lot of Suno-generated tracks is that a lot of the time, you’ll hear the vocals and other melodic elements will start stuttering at the same exact time,” Harris explained. “These models still have a hard time fully separating different parts of the songs they’re trained on, and they treat these elements like one big instrument. As a music producer, all of these things come across like choices that a human just wouldn’t make with their compositions because it just doesn’t make sense.”

In some instances, the visuals accompanying AI tracks are part of what prompts Harris to accuse people of slinging AI. You might not be able to hear the generative models behind evangelical Christian AI persona Lionsaddle’s music, but you can clearly see the character’s fingers vanishing in and out of existence in videos. There is also an overly glossy visual quality to most of the videos posted by Christian house musician Midnite Manna that makes their content look a lot like what we typically refer to as AI slop.

Suno also came up multiple times during my conversation with 39-year-old Italian turntabilist-turned-producer Nihil Young. Young’s posts on Threads about people using Suno are what initially inspired Harris to make his videos. Like Harris, Young has spent the past few months watching multiple EDM newcomers’ stars rise after they post music he thinks was generated with AI tools like Suno’s. And while Young isn’t usually one to get involved with online discourse, he felt it was important to speak out about how many people are flooding the scene with AI tracks.

“These songs are the sound of Suno, which to me means that the people behind the songs are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking the platform to remix them,” Young told me, referring to Josh Fawaz’s “Like a Prayer” cover, which now includes AI credits following a wave of online backlash. “If they can do it with major artists like her, they can do it with you, me, and everyone else, which just isn’t cool. They can take your entire catalog, feed it to Suno, and generate ‘new’ songs from that stolen work.”

Young claimed that in response to his Threads posts, he received multiple hacking attempts and a wave of online harassment from AI defenders. He also told me that he thinks people bought fake followers to boost his Spotify numbers as a way of casting doubt on his authenticity. That spooked Young — who is raising a young daughter and just put out a new album of his own — to rethink whether he should continue. He’s taken a break from callouts, but he still thinks it’s important to know about the way AI music is harming human artists.

“Music production is where most of my income comes from, and almost as soon as AI began rolling out, I started losing many of my clients,” said Young, who has previously done audio mixing and mastering work for Sony Music, Warner, and Universal. “I can only imagine what it’s been like for singers, graphics artists, and people working in other creative fields. Whether you realize it or not, this stuff is impacting everyone.”

What Young wishes more listeners could appreciate is how easy it has become to generate entire songs with platforms like Suno. In his opinion, most people using AI to make music “aren’t actually doing anything creative and they don’t have a true artistic process” because many generative tools on the market involve some degree of autogeneration. When I brought up how detailed AI prompts can be, he insisted that many of the people posting AI music likely aren’t even writing their own inputs. Young noted that Suno’s Simple Mode allows users to whip up songs by simply selecting a musical genre and clicking a button — a process that requires basically zero thinking. (Suno has not responded to a request for comment in time for publication.)

“I also think that a lot of people these days are consuming music like fast food.”

Aside from the people uploading all of these songs, no one has a way of being absolutely certain whether the tracks were generated with AI or made by an actual artist. AI music detection tools are one potential solution, but it’s not entirely clear how and, perhaps more importantly, if listeners might incorporate them into their lives. Judging by the numbers (which, of course, can be manipulated with paid streams), there do seem to be people who don’t mind the sounds of Suno and other AI tools. Young knows that most people’s ears probably aren’t well-attuned to identifying audio slop, but he still thinks that music lovers owe it to themselves to make the effort to find real, human artists.

“In my opinion, it becomes obvious that you’re listening to AI-generated music when you put on a good pair of headphones,” Young told me. “But I also think that a lot of people these days are consuming music like fast food and listening to it through the speakers on their phone. Or they just have it on a background noise, and they don’t necessarily care what it sounds like.”

Tech.title: Google further buries search results under AI mode
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Google is now automatically expanding its AI search summaries at the top of the results page for some searches, as reported by Search Engine Roundtable. The change, when it kicks in, pushes the typical list of links from a search much farther down Google’s results page; instead of seeing part of an AI Overview with a “Show more” button you can click, you’ll Google will show a full AI Overview at the top of your search, an “Ask anything” box under that, and then the list of links. It can lead to a lot of scrolling.

It’s unclear exactly what Google’s criteria is for the auto-expanding AI Overviews. Before writing this story, I was seeing them with most of my test searches. But now, AI Overviews usually just show the initial part of the response and the “Show more” button. My most consistent query to get the auto-expanding AI Overview is “what is the best game on switch 2”, but even that hasn’t been consistent across searches and browsers.

“For some queries, AI Overviews may dynamically expand for topics where our systems determine it’s most useful for people,” Google spokesperson Jennifer Kutz says in a statement to The Verge. “Our research has shown that with this dynamic experience, users find Search more helpful and engage deeper in follow-up exploration.” Kutz also says that “If users have already begun scrolling to view content below the AI Overview, we cancel expansion so that the user doesn’t lose their reading position.”

Tech.title: Xbox CEO calls Project Helix a ‘family of devices’
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, Project Helix, which she announced in March as a codename for Microsoft’s “next generation console” — phrasing that seemingly implied a singular device — will actually be a “family” of devices.”

“We’ve been hard at work on a great next generation and a great family of devices for Helix, and we’ll share more soon,” Sharma told BBC News. She shared the answer after being asked if Helix will be a discless console. She didn’t answer that, but this week Microsoft announced a program for digitizing your physical games.

In 2025, Microsoft and AMD announced a “strategic multi-year partnership” to work together on “a portfolio of devices,” including Microsoft’s next-generation console, so it seems likely the two companies are also partnering on this family of Helix devices in some way. It’s been rumored that third parties will be able to sell Project Helix devices of their own — a rumor that Xbox’s VP of next generation, Jason Ronald, didn’t exactly deny when he wrote that: “Project Helix will be available as a 1st party Xbox console.”

It’s unclear when Project Helix, which will be able to play PC games, might actually launch. In February, shortly before Sharma’s surprise appointment to the top job at Xbox, AMD hinted that it would be ready to support a launch of Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox in 2027, and at a conference in March, Ronald said that Helix wouldn’t reach alpha until 2027.

Tech.title: Save hundreds on a TCL mini-LED TV with quantum dots and high refresh rate
Tech.content: Amazon and Best Buy have the TCL QM7L mini-LED TV on sale for as low as $797.99 for the 55-inch model, a $200 discount from the usual price. We spotted scaling discounts on larger sizes as well, although Amazon already listed low stock on the 65-inch version. While OLED televisions are great for deep black levels and great contrast, their high price point may be off-putting to some buyers. Mini-LED TVs like this TCL are a more wallet-friendly option, and have high brightness while also supporting features like Quantum Dots for vivid colors.

Tech.title: Sony Music, Warner sue Anthropic, alleging a “brazen campaign” of intellectual property theft
Tech.content:
In Brief
